title: The hacks introverts are using to survive and thrive in the RTO era
description: For some introverts, quiet office corners and empty conference rooms have become safe havens from overstimulation.
fullText:
As offices get more crowded, introverts are re-adjusting to in-person working life.

Employees share the hacks they use to conserve energy, including finding quiet office hideaways.

Some companies, like Cisco or KPMG, are redesigning office spaces to accommodate worker preferences.

Scouring the office for an empty conference room. Spending lunch on an outdoor bench for a few minutes of quiet. Stacking meetings into one part of the day so you can spend the rest uninterrupted.

If you identify as an introvert, these habits may sound familiar.

Introverts make up roughly 40 to 50% of the workforce, though estimates vary, organizational psychologist Anique van der Putten told Business Insider. They typically prefer lower levels of external stimulation and need time alone to recharge after prolonged social interaction or other highly stimulating experiences, she said.

During the pandemic, many white-collar introverts were able to enjoy a setup that played to their strengths: remote work. Now, as employers double down on return-to-office mandates and tighten hybrid policies, offices are filling up again and introverts are relearning how to navigate workplaces that reward interaction, visibility, and spontaneous collaboration.

Pandemic-era remote work introduced workers to the possibility of a new arrangement, with less background noise, fewer unplanned conversations, and reduced pressure to remain socially available throughout the day, Nargiza Noimann-Zander, a clinical psychologist and neuroscience researcher, told Business Insider.

"Returning to the office can therefore feel more intense than it did before, because people have now experienced an alternative," wrote Noimann-Zander via email.

Although return-to-office mandates have been in place for some time, office attendance has continued to climb and is now near its post-pandemic high, with weekly office occupancy averaging about 52.5%, according to data from physical security and property technology company Kastle.

Linda Le, a tech recruiter who describes herself as a "proud introvert" on LinkedIn, said that the transition back to in-person work felt overwhelming, especially since her job already requires a lot of interaction. She said at first she "cried a lot" and felt overstimulated due to the constant background noise and interruptions.

"I remember I went to a room and I had a panic attack," Le said.

Some workers have developed rituals to manage feeling overstimulated. Charles Broomfield, a 26-year-old engineering analyst at Google, said he keeps his headphones on during the day and prefers to eat meals alone, unless someone asks to join him.

"I like the quiet time and that space and that recharge," said Broomfield, who goes to the office five days a week.

Catherine Fadashe, who works in marketing and communications in London, said returning to the office in 2023 was a "huge adjustment." These days, after working in person, she spends an hour in complete silence and avoiding social media to decompress. On the three days a week she goes in, she imagines she's about to go onstage.

"As the lift doors are opening, I feel like, 'this is my entrance,'" Fadashe previously told Business Insider. "I have a mental countdown."

As more workers return to the office, a number of companies, including KPMG and Superhuman, are redesigning offices to better support different working styles — and make employees want to spend more time in them.

Data from Kastle shows that office attendance is nearly 20% higher in what it calls "A+ office buildings," or those with newer offices with modern designs and premium amenities.

Cisco redesigned its London office to accommodate neurodiverse workers and installed a soundproof wellness room with no technology for employees who want a break from screens. Bob Cicero, a workplace director at Cisco who specializes in smart buildings and real-estate, said that employees hang out there after their commute to "reset their minds."

Stephanie Miller, a spokesperson for Hok, a design firm that implements offices that support various working needs, told Business Insider that office design fundamentally impacts productivity.

"If you can find the environment that supports your sensory levels and allows you to not be distracted by the noise, the smell, the pattern, you're going to be able to be more focused and more productive," Miller said.

Kelly Dubisar, a design director at Gensler, which has designed offices for companies including Nvidia, said the firm has seen growing demand since the pandemic for offices that support a wider range of working styles.

Newer offices may include dedicated collaboration spaces, quiet focus rooms with dim lighting, and flexible work areas that give workers more control over noise and stimulation. Gensler's 2026 Workplace Survey, based on responses from over 16,000 full-time office-based workers, suggests that employees are more likely to view their workplace as effective when they offer manageable noise levels, flexible furniture, updated technology, and spaces for focused work and rest.

Gensler's San Francisco office, features a wide variety of furniture and lighting options to address specific sensory needs. It also has setups to support different thermal and acoustic preferences. For example, one of its areas, called The Vault, has a deep-focus quiet space that is dark and conversation-free.

For some workers, those types of quiet corners and ooms have become a refuge. Erin Mantz, a communications worker, said that the "nooks and crannies and quiet rooms" in the various offices she's worked at since the pandemic help her focus.

Van der Putten said that some people make the assumption that introverts are shy or anxious, but that's not necessarily true. While many introverts told Business Insider they enjoyed a quiet space to recharge at work, most weren't asking for offices to become silent and enjoyed collaborating with coworkers face-to-face. However, they wanted control over when those interactions happened and space to recharge afterward.

"I don't dread going to the office," Le said, adding that she chats with her coworkers throughout the day, and goes to quiet spaces when she wants to focus or hop on calls.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: White House wants veterans to replace immigrant truckers who lost their licenses in crackdown
description: The Trump administration wants soldiers to consider becoming truck drivers when they leave the military to help replace the tens of thousands of immigrant drivers who lost their licenses in a crackdow...
fullText:
The Trump administration wants soldiers to consider becoming truck drivers when they leave the military to help replace the tens of thousands of immigrant drivers who lost their licenses in a crackdown this year.

A new campaign launched Friday will promote programs that let veterans who recently drove large military vehicles skip the required skills test for a commercial driver's license. Other soldiers can attend a commercial driving school during their last six months of active duty. The GI Bill will also pay for 100% of commercial driver's license training and for some people even pay a housing allowance while they are in school.

The campaign will be part of a broader interagency effort to help veterans find good civilian jobs that the White House plans to announce on Monday.

The Transportation Department began enforcing existing English language requirements for truckers last summer. Concerns about truck driver qualifications then took on more urgency after an August crash in Florida, when a truck driver performed an illegal U-turn that killed three people. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that driver, who is from India, should never have been licensed in the first place.

Audits conducted in every state uncovered numerous non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses that remained valid long after an immigrant's work permits had expired or were issued without properly verifying their citizenship status.

Since then, about 26,000 drivers have been pulled off the road for failing to demonstrate English proficiency, and the Transportation Department said 30,000 commercial licenses were canceled because they were issued illegally. The federal government has tried to withhold millions of dollars of highway funds from California and New York for failing to comply and revoke thousands more licenses, but that has wound up in court. Several other states — including Pennsylvania, Minnesota and North Carolina — have been warned they are at risk of losing funding.

"We are removing more and more dangerous foreign drivers off our roads every day and restoring the integrity of America's trucking industry," Duffy said. "Our new Freedom Haulers campaign will help build on these successes and get the word out that there's never been a better time for America's former service members to get behind the wheel of a big rig."

The trucking industry has applauded the administration's effort to get unqualified drivers off the road and close down sham CDL schools, and companies praised this new effort to get more veterans behind the wheel.

"Veterans make up 15% of our workforce and bring the highest levels of leadership, discipline and technical skills that are essential to our success. We are dedicated to providing them with meaningful careers and a supportive environment where they can thrive," said Derek Leathers, who is chairman and CEO of Werner Enterprises.

Cole Stevens, who is chief strategy officer at the trucking company that bears his last name, said veterans' backgrounds make them great drivers.

"Some of the best drivers and industry leaders I've had the privilege of working with are military veterans," Stevens said. "Their integrity, accountability, and mission-first mindset make them an incredible asset."

In addition to enforcing existing restrictions, the government announced plans to restrict which immigrants can qualify for a non-domiciled commercial driver's license and require them to take the test in English, but those rules are being challenged in court.

The only immigrant drivers who can get a license under the new rules are holders of an H-2A, H-2A or E-2 visa. H-2A is for temporary agricultural workers while H-2B is for temporary nonagricultural workers, and E-2 is for people who make substantial investments in a U.S. business.

Immigrants account for about 20% of all truck drivers, but all of these non-domiciled licenses for immigrants represent only about 5% of all commercial driver's licenses, or about 200,000 drivers.

Some immigrant groups have said they believe that many drivers are being unfairly targeted. The spotlight has been on Sikh truckers because the driver in the Florida crash and the driver in another fatal crash in California in October are both Sikh.

The Transportation Department plans to work with the Pentagon and Departments of Veterans Affairs and Labor to promote the career field as a good job that offers independence to veterans who don't want a desk job in civilian life.

Veterans still have to study the rules and pass the written test for a commercial driver's license, but soldiers who recently drove big military vehicles over 2.5 tons (2.25 metric tons) can skip the skills test. The government said more than 40,000 veterans have already used that program, which can enable them to get on the road within a few weeks.

The Transportation Department said that truck drivers currently make an average of $70,000 a year, as the truck market has tightened up and rates have increased.

Veterans who served for at least three years can also use the money from the GI Bill program to pay for CDL training, and they might even qualify for a housing stipend.

title: Trump administration faces record turnover in second term
description: More Senate-confirmed officials have left President Donald Trump’s second administration in its first 18 months than they have during the same period in other 21st century administrations, according t...
fullText:
More Senate-confirmed officials have left President Donald Trump's second administration in its first 18 months than they have during the same period in other 21st century administrations, according to a nonpartisan organization's review of the turnover published Wednesday.

The review from Partnership for Public Service, a group that focuses on improving the federal government, found that as of Monday, 27 Senate-confirmed officials in Cabinet departments have departed the administration — a figure that outpaces the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump's first administration, which was known for its turnover.

The departures impacted 13 departments and included three Cabinet secretaries: Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Attorney General Pam Bondi and Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer. Other high-profile officials that have left include Secretary of the Navy John Phelan and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Susan Monarez.

The review also found that the administration is slow to fill the vacancies with Trump sending fewer nominations to the Senate than even his first term. It does not include US attorneys, US marshals or ambassadors who have left or nominations for those positions.

"Turnover on this scale does not just thin the government's leadership ranks—it concentrates power in the president," Chris Piper of the Partnership for Public Service wrote in a blog post. "Left unaddressed, more of the government will be led by officials installed without the Senate's constitutionally required advice and consent, and it will be less able to do the work Americans depend on."

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said in a statement to CNN, "President Trump has the most talented Cabinet in American history who work every day to implement his common sense, America First agenda. In just over one year, the President and his Cabinet have made our country greater than ever before with the most secure border in history, the largest middle-class tax cut ever, and the lowest murder rate since 1900. The President and his entire administration will continue to tirelessly implement the Trump agenda and achieve tremendous results for the American people."

While every president has appointed officials in "acting" capacity, which temporarily avoids the Senate confirmation process, Trump has done so more frequently and openly, CNN has previously reported.

During his first term, Trump said, "Acting gives you much greater flexibility. A lot easier to do things."

This headline has been updated.

title: The UK’s first TikTok PM? Andy Burnham channels Zohran Mamdani as he hits social media

fullText:
From Mo Farah to Bus Aunty, new prime minister makes good on promise to ‘do things differently’ when it comes to communication

They say a week is a long time in politics, but handily for followers of Andy Burnham on social media, you can get daily updates of what the new PM has been up to on his timeline.

Before Burnham stepped inside No 10 this week he promised to “do things differently” in British politics. If his feed is anything to go by, he’s already way ahead of his predecessor.

Burnham’s social media team have done away with the buttoned-up operation of Keir Starmer, opting instead for a style that has already drawn comparisons to another much more “online” politician: the mayor of New York, Zohran Mamdani.

Burnham’s TikTok page this week has revealed him to be a man (or at least a man who pays someone) who enjoys a meme, someone who comments with emojis, collaborates with influencers and chats policy while pouring a pint.

Noticeable were the policy announcements shot in primarily vertical videos, ideal for mobile phone consumption on TikTok, Facebook and Instagram.

“He’s gone all in on the TikTok style,” said Andrew Chadwick, professor of political communication at Loughborough University. “So far, he’s had some very simple, clear policy pledges that cut through.”

During the lead-up to his first day in No 10, Burnham’s team also released a 2.5-minute video of Burnham inviting people in Cardiff to “ask Andy anything” from addressing homelessness and social care to supporting pubs and the hospitality sector.

Searches for “Andy Burnham” on TikTok surged by more than 2,000% day on day in the UK when he became prime minister on Monday.

Burnham started off his first day with a handheld video outside a centre for the London-based homelessness charity The Passage, promising to end rough sleeping “at the first opportunity”. A “day one” montage posted later on, showing him inside The Passage, meeting his cabinet and speaking outside No 10, received more than 820,000 views.

His team also posted two prepackaged videos starring influencers and celebrities. Burnham joined Sir Mo Farah for a jog through London as part of the gold medallist’s YouTube series Run With Mo, which was reposted on Farah’s Instagram to his 1.9 million followers.

Social media is about content, of course but it’s also a numbers game. Burnham’s team showed that when they had him take part in the viral Career Ladder series, hosted by Ukrainian internet personality Max Klymenko, who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.

These collaboration deals offer Burnham “exposure” to new audiences and build a “constructed sense of authenticity” on the platform, said Chadwick. “Burnham has a brand to construct here. OK, big in the north-west of England, absolutely. But among most people, who don’t follow politics particularly closely, he’s got hard work to do.”

The world of social media is all about taking ideas and riffing on them – and imitation is, after all, the sincerest form of flattery, but one video from Burnham’s first week of posts showed just the kind of online profile he’d like to emulate.

The PM’s video on Wednesday, announcing his plans to cut VAT on energy bills – one of the more eye-catching in his week one policy blitz – received more than 1m views. Keen-eyed political watchers, however, spotted a similarity between his announcement video and one posted by Zohran Mamdani some months back.

The video, which starts with Burnham tapping the camera and stepping backward, references a video by Mamdani who in April used the same move to announce his pied-à-terre tax.

Those behind Mamdani’s digital strategy have taken note. “I think it’s great that he’s not shying away from these direct, creative references, while also doing some creative things of his own,” said Debbie Saslaw, co-founder of the political ad agency Melted Solids with Anthony DiMieri.

But Saslaw also has a warning for Burnham: “I saw, during the campaign, he jumped on a lot of Instagram meme trends. Stay away from that. That’s something that becomes automatically cringe, no matter who does it.”

In his first week as PM, Burnham’s TikTok following rose by approximately 73%, from just under 99,000 to more than 170,000, according to consultancy Knox Digital. In terms of engagement, Burnham narrowly beat Starmer’s first week on TikTok in December 2025, at 6.29% to the previous PM’s 6.23%.

“There is an authentic style that comes through” in Burnham’s videos, said Andrew Bard Epstein, the communications director on Mamdani’s election campaign. “Where it feels different, substantively, from Zohran is the ambition of the agenda.”

He added: “In terms of style and authenticity, he is clearing the very low bar left by Keir Starmer. But unless it is matched with some stronger stuff – on confronting concentrated power, inequality and a diminishing quality of life in a way that feels like it meets the scale of the crisis – I wonder if people may grow tired of it.”

title: ‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPT
description:
Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?
As a small boy growing up in Amritsar, India, in the 1960s, Avtar Singh used to hear whispers. Your mum isn’t really your mum, the rumours would say.
fullText:
As a small boy growing up in Amritsar, India, in the 1960s, Avtar Singh used to hear whispers. Your mum isn’t really your mum, the rumours would say. Your mum lives abroad. Avtar didn’t really pay any attention to it. “I thought, the neighbours are just making up stories.” But the stories were true: the woman raising Avtar was actually his grandmother. When he was too young to remember it, his father had emigrated to Canada to work as a teacher, leaving Avtar in the care of his paternal grandparents. His grandfather, a police officer, was a fearsome authoritarian, but his grandmother brought him up with tenderness, as if he were her own son. She called him by his nickname, Titu. He felt loved.

When Avtar was around eight years old, he was told about his family in Canada: his dad, his mum and a little brother were waiting for him there, and he would soon travel to join them. Just after his ninth birthday, Avtar found himself sitting on a plane, dressed in a three‑piece suit and tie. He was travelling alone. He had never flown before. He didn’t speak a word of English. He landed in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Christmas Eve, 1968; his family met him at the airport and took him home. “I didn’t know what to think,” Avtar, now 66, tells me in a video call from his home in Abbotsford, British Columbia. “Before I knew it, it was the first week of January, and I was put in school.”

Unable to communicate with any of the other pupils, Avtar watched what they did and followed along, storing his snow boots in the cloakroom, standing up to sing the Canadian national anthem and God Save the Queen. But with his long hair tied in the topknot often worn by Sikh boys, he stood out. His parents offered to buy him a hockey stick and a pair of ice skates if he agreed to get his hair cut. He learned English. His nickname changed from Titu to the more Canadian “Tito”. He began to blend in.

But Avtar didn’t fit in at home. He was much paler than everyone else – “the white sheep of the family,” he jokes. And they treated him like an outsider, an afterthought. When he was 14, his family went on holiday without him, leaving Avtar home alone for two weeks. He got on well enough with his father, but didn’t gel at all with his mother. “She didn’t have any of the warmth that my grandma had. She absolutely hated me.” She seemed much more like a stepmother than a mother.

That feeling was confirmed when Avtar got married and his grandparents flew over to stay with him and his new wife, Rosie. His grandma “whispered into my wife’s ear” that Avtar was the product of his father’s first marriage. “She didn’t say what my mother’s name was. She just said, ‘Her family was from Africa, and she left the child with us and went back to Africa. She might have gone to live in the UK.’ That’s it.” It didn’t feel right to ask his grandparents 

When his son was set a school assignment to complete his family tree, Avtar felt emboldened to approach his father. “I said, ‘Dad, you’ve got to tell me at least what my mother’s name was.’” His dad eventually relented: her first name was Savinder. But he would not give Avtar any more information, no matter how many times he asked. “I was stonewalled.” Avtar had no idea why his parents had split up. “All I really understood was that my mother’s family encouraged her to give up custody of me so it would be easier for them to remarry her.”

He thought about his mother constantly. When Rosie was pregnant with their daughter, there were anomalies in some of the antenatal tests, and Rosie and Avtar were referred to a geneticist. Avtar was asked about his parents’ medical history. “I couldn’t tell them anything about my mother’s family history. It hit me right in the heart. That’s when I thought, I’ve got to do something.”

He Googled and Facebooked, but there was almost nothing to go on; Savinder is a fairly common Punjabi Sikh name. In 2009, Avtar flew to London to visit the National Archives at Kew with the hope of finding immigration or marriage records that might lead him to his mother. “I couldn’t find anything at all.” On a later visit to London, he emailed Sunrise Radio, a British Asian station, asking if they could put out an appeal to find his mother, but they told Avtar they don’t do that kind of thing, out of respect for people’s privacy. That gave Avtar pause. “I thought, maybe I should just cool off. If my mother has some other family, I don’t want to disrupt her life.” Still, it niggled. Three or four years ago, he asked a British south Asian work colleague for advice; she suggested contacting the ITV show Long Lost Family. He watched a few episodes and decided it wasn’t for him. But he longed to know his mother. “The thought of her did not leave my mind, ever.”

The one thing Avtar did not do was a DNA test. He is retired now, but he used to be a chartered accountant, and he knows enough about technology, data and privacy to be wary of giving up his genetic code to a corporation. “They can sell it. Not only that – if they see something in my DNA, that affects my kids. I don’t want that information up there.” He deactivated his Facebook account 12 years ago for similar reasons. “I don’t have faith that these companies have the proper safeguards.”

Then, on 8 May this year, Avtar and Rosie were on holiday in the south of France. Avtar had been battling cancer; their long-awaited trip to Europe came after he had finished his treatment. “It was early morning, and I had read all the news. I was bored. I had nothing else to do. I thought, I’ve tried Google and everything else, why don’t I give AI a shot?”

He typed a prompt into ChatGPT, based on the little he knew, and what else he could infer. He assumed that his mother would be around the same age as his father (who died 10 years ago); he knew that Sikh women of her generation were generally given the middle name Kaur.

Avtar Can you find any information about a Savinder Kaur?

Avtar She would be between 87 and 97 years old and would have lived in India and Africa and possibly in the UK

ChatGPT The strongest match, based upon your clues, is this …

ChatGPT Savinder Kaur Nagi, born in 1936 in Kisumu, Kenya, to Indian Sikh parents.

ChatGPT The article mentions family roots near Jammu and Kashmir in India and later migration connections to the UK.

“I know that AI can just make up shit. So I thought, OK, that’s nice says Avtar. “But it actually referenced an article. I thought, I’ll look at that, at least. Just to see.”

“I wrote it out of grief,” Nicci Dhamu tells me, in a cafe in west London. “Mummy never really had a voice, and that article was all about giving her one. I wanted to create a digital legacy for my mum.”

Nicci is the jewellery designer behind the brand Sohavi. “Sohavi means beautiful in Gurmukhī, the Sikh script. I learned about making things beautiful from Mum.” Her article, published on both the Sohavi blog and the South Asian Heritage Month website, was a celebration of her mother’s creativity. “She suffered loss, and decisions were made for her when she young and wasn’t able to assert her own voice, like many south Asian women of her generation. But she lives on through me and the profound influences she had on me throughout my life,” Nicci wrote.

Savinder Kaur Nagi died in her sleep in December 2024, aged 88. For the last five years of her life, she had dementia. Nicci, 58, had been her carer; they lived together and were very close. Nicci’s family moved to the UK from Kenya in 1973. She has an older sister and a younger brother, as well as three half-sisters from her dad’s first marriage; he was widowed before he met Savinder. “We grew up as one family. I didn’t know until I was about 10 or 11 years old that my sisters were my half‑sisters, and that was only because one of my sisters told me.” Theirs was a family that did not speak about the past.

“I remember once, Mum was in the kitchen making roti, and I asked her, ‘Mummy, you were, like, 25 years old when you got married to Dad. Wasn’t that a little old for somebody of your generation?’ I knew that something was different about our family, but I didn’t have the vocabulary to label it. My father never spoke to us about his wife who had died, and my mum never spoke about her life before him.”

When Nicci was in her 40s, an older cousin casually revealed that Savinder had been married to another man before she met Nicci’s dad. “She was married off, very young. And it probably wasn’t what she wanted,” Nicci tells me. “My grandfather took her and her sisters out of school in Kenya and took them back to Punjab to a place called Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar.” Later in life, her mother would openly lament leaving school – she could read and write English, and loved studying – but never explained why she had been forced to give up her education. She did not discuss her first marriage. She never told her children they had an older half-brother.

“My cousin told me in that conversation that she had a son.” Nicci’s eyes are bright at the memory. But she never felt able to ask her mother about him. “I couldn’t. There was intrinsic pain there.”

There were times, Nicci says, when her mother would sink into a depression. “She would sit quietly, or take to bed because she was upset.” Nicci would bring Savinder her dinner, and encourage her to sit up and eat. “Towards the end of Mum’s life, she used to cry, ‘Mera bacha’ [‘My child’, in Punjabi]. The dementia was bringing up all these memories for her.”

It was then – a couple of years before her mum’s death – that Nicci resolved to find the child her mother was crying for. But she did not know his name, and her mother was unwell so Nicci couldn’t ask her. Instead, she turned to her wider family.

She began with her mother’s young brother, who lives in Birmingham. “He knew my mum’s child as a two- or three-year-old,” Nicci says. She picked his brains, and also her cousins’. She learned that her mother’s first husband was called Mohan Singh, a very educated man who taught at the Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school in Amritsar. Mohan’s father had been a police officer, and “quite a difficult man”. Savinder had told her father that her husband wasn’t treating her well. “I think my grandad thought, this is not a good place for my daughter to be. He went around and took his daughter back to his home, and she must have picked up her little boy, too.”

Her mother raised the boy until he was three years old, Nicci was told. “As someone who is also divorced, I often reflect on the stigma my mother may have faced as a south Asian woman of her generation,” she tells me. “I think there was a lot of pressure from the family: let’s get her married. Somebody as young as her was going to have a very difficult life as a single mother. She was too young to be on her own. Her son’s family wanted him back. So they must have taken the child from her.”

Savinder returned to Kenya, alone. At first, she stayed with her eldest brother. Nicci’s cousins have vivid memories of her time in their home. “She would take his baby clothes out and cry. She never forgot him.” She was soon introduced to Nicci’s father, a man 16 years her senior. “I think she carried that trauma throughout her life, but did a very good job of holding her head up high, making her life work, raising three more children.” Family in Kenya heard “through the grapevine” that Savinder’s first husband had moved to Canada, but they couldn’t tell Nicci when. And no one knew the name of Savinder’s little boy. They only knew his nickname: Titu.

“No one’s going to call themselves Titu on LinkedIn, are they?” says Nicci with a deep laugh. That didn’t stop her trying to find him online, and his father and grandfather, too, Googling the names of teachers and police officers in Amritsar. “I didn’t capture anything. How do you find somebody without a name? It’s impossible.”

Three or four months before her mother died, she submitted Savinder’s DNA to Ancestry.com. “I set up a profile for her, saying, ‘Profile managed by daughter, looking for her son, name is Titu, possibly living in Canada.’” She got some interesting titbits back about her mother’s ancestral roots in Kashmir, Afghanistan and Uzbekistan, which would explain her light complexion, but no useful matches.

A month after her mother died, Nicci contacted friends who knew people who had worked for the magistrates court in Amritsar, in the hope of finding records of the divorce. “If there were divorce papers, there would be names – and maybe a child’s name.” But she was told that would be virtually impossible; a needle in a haystack.

In April 2025, Nicci’s family took Savinder’s ashes to India. During her stay in Amritsar, Nicci hired a driver to take her to Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school, where Titu’s father had been a teacher. She spoke to the teachers and the security guard, but it was long after Mohan Singh’s time there, so no one knew of him or his son. All she wanted was a name for her half-brother, but no one could tell her. It felt hopeless.

“I remember sitting there thinking, why doesn’t he just knock on the door? I knew that his father was an educated man – I was pretty sure that he must be educated, too. Why isn’t he looking for Mum?”

Avtar blinked at the article ChatGPT had presented to him. Rosie was just waking up. He made her a coffee and showed her what he’d found, but she wasn’t convinced. After all, the article didn’t mention Savinder’s first marriage, divorce or long-lost son. “Rosie didn’t want me to be disappointed – she knows how hard I had looked for my mother.”

Then he looked at the article again, and a picture stopped him in his tracks: not one of the many photos Nicci had posted of her mother – there was no flicker of instant recognition when he saw Savinder’s face – but an image of a certificate her mother had earned for dressmaking at a college in Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar, in 1962. (“She was so proud of it,” Nicci beams. “She would talk about it quite often: ‘I went to college, I earned a certificate.’ I think that was her quiet victory.”)

“This is two or three years after I was born, and it is in the exact city where I was born.” Avtar exhales deeply, as if he still can’t believe what he saw. He had to find out more. “This is the closest I’ve ever come. It would be a shame to just stop here.”

At 8.36am that morning, he sent Nicci an email, thanking her for writing the tribute to her mother.

Avtar What especially resonated with me was the part of her life connected to India. Reading about her journey raised many personal questions and reflections for me, and I found myself feeling there may be some distant family or community connections between us.

Avtar I want to assure you that I am not reaching out for any business, financial, or other formal reason, only in the spirit of a friendly conversation.

Nicci had spent the previous night praying at the gurdwara and watching Long Lost Family on TV. Avtar’s email had arrived on the morning of what would have been her mother’s 90th birthday. “It was wild!” Nicci exclaims. “I just had a real sense of knowing. I can’t explain it. This is my mum’s son. It’s got to be.”

She agonised over how to reply, eventually adopting a similarly friendly but respectful tone.

Nicci I am equally intrigued to know if there might be a family connection. I would be happy to have a conversation with you.

Her phone number was in her email signature. Avtar sent her a message on WhatsApp as soon as he saw it, asking when they could speak. Nicci scrutinised his WhatsApp profile picture. “He had a very distinctive nose. Everybody in my mother’s family has this prominent, distinguished nose.” She messaged back – she was free to talk there and then.

It was barely two hours since Avtar had typed his prompt into ChatGPT. He was driving with Rosie to get some croissants for breakfast. He parked up, clicked on Nicci’s number and called her. There wasn’t much of a preamble. Avtar was too eager to have his questions finally answered.

Avtar Good morning! This is Avtar Singh

Avtar When Is a good time to talk

Nicci I’m London based. As you probably know.

“Can you tell me a bit about your mother’s time in India?” he asked.

“Mummy was married and divorced in India,” Nicci replied.

“Yes,” Nicci said. “She had a son.”

Both Avtar and Rosie burst into tears.

“Titu, is that you?” asked Nicci. “Are you Titu, my mother’s son?”

“Yes,” Avtar replied. “That’s who I am. But I haven’t heard anyone pronounce my nickname that way since my grandma called me that, when I was a little boy.”

“At that moment, time just froze,” Avtar remembers. “But I quickly recovered. I said, ‘You’re my sister. Holy shit – are there more of you out there?’ It had never occurred to me that my mother would have a family, and that I could actually meet them. That family, they knew about me – everybody knew about me, they just wouldn’t talk about it – but I had no knowledge about them whatsoever.”

They spoke for two hours in that first phone call, until Avtar’s battery started to die. Nicci had assumed he must be in Canada; she couldn’t believe he was in France, so close by. “Why don’t you fly over?” she asked. Avtar’s head was spinning. They agreed to speak again later that evening, in a video call.

Avtar This was a dream of a lifetime!

Nicci then gave Avtar a tour of the family photos displayed in the living room she used to share with their mother. “I was just sharing everything I could with him. And sobbing. And remembering Mum. All that grief about her yearning to see him again, and not meeting him. It’s like the universe just flung something at me – although I’ve lost my mum, I’ve gained a brother.”

When Avtar told his son the news, he urged him to go to London and meet his newfound family. By the time he reached his daughter, she already knew: she had been using Avtar’s ChatGPT account and had seen his search history. “She said to me, ‘Dad, if you do not go see her now, you’re going to come back home and that’s all you’re going to think about. So go now.’”

Within days, Avtar and Rosie were in London. Nicci shows me a picture of the first time they met, at a hotel near Heathrow. Their faces are flushed with joy. “I could see the raw emotion in her – she had been looking for me for so long,” Avtar says. “When I met her and hugged her tight, I thought, yes, this is my sister.” They went out for dinner and compared stories and timelines, piecing together the fragments that their families had given them.

The following morning, Nicci took Avtar and Rosie to Birmingham, to meet their mother’s last-surviving sibling – their uncle – who had once shared a home with baby Titu. “He looked at me and said, ‘I remember you. I held you in my arms,’” Avtar tells me, his eyes awash with tears. “It was a great, great visit.”

The next day, Avtar was introduced to his half‑brother – Nicci’s youngest sibling. He had been shocked when Nicci first told him she had found Avtar. “He said, ‘But I’m Mummy’s son,’” Nicci tells me, laughing. “I said, ‘Of course you are. Nothing’s going to change our family.’ When they finally met, Nicci says her younger brother shook Avtar’s hand. “I just knew it was going to be all right. My brother said, ‘I’ve always wanted a big brother.’”

Avtar and Nicci both tell me they have no plans to confirm their relationship with a DNA test. There’s no need, they say.

“This world has a few billion people in it. And if somebody can randomly call me Titu … ” Avtar shakes his head. “I don’t think I need any more verification than that.”

The joy at finally finding Titu is bittersweet for Nicci, because it came too late for her mother. “My biggest regret is that I didn’t talk to her about her son and let her cry about him, let her have a release,” she tells me. “It wasn’t her fault. It wasn’t anything that she did wrong. It just was a marriage that broke down.”

“I grew up believing that she gave me up because it was the best thing to help her move on with her life. I was OK with that. I thought, I hope that she had a good life. I’m not the type of person to grieve or feel bad that I got abandoned or anything like that,” Avtar says. “Now I’ve heard from Nicci and other people in the family that my mum used to cry for me. That’s all I need to hear. It just feels so good to know that I was loved.”

Plus, Avtar adds, there is “the treasure my mother left behind for me – I have all this family to get to know”. Word about Avtar is slowly spreading across the globe. He’s in a WhatsApp group for his maternal family, including cousins based in Kenya; they have seen each other on FaceTime. There’s discussion of a trip to Kenya so Avtar can meet them in the flesh, and see where Savinder once lived.

“My cousins are so excited to meet him. He looks like them – same smiles, bald and bearded,” Nicci says with another throaty laugh. She whips out her phone to show me an AI-generated image Avtar has made of himself arm in arm with two cousins he’s yet to meet in person. Technology is bringing Savinder’s family together in ways she could never have envisaged, or even imagined.

“We had a video call last night,” Nicci says. “Every time I see him, I look at him and I just want to cry. That’s my brother. It’s so natural to want to have him in our lives.” She pauses. “Who would have thought that life would unfold in this way? That ChatGPT would find an article that would lead to an email that would lead to all of this? Technology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be sometimes. There is a human touch to AI – look what happened.”

Her half-brother sees things differently. “Right now, AI is still a glorified search engine. It is a piece of software that recognises a pattern in a string of characters, and it can look at millions of responses that match that character set and give you the highest probability best answer. What did it do? It looked at a couple of character strings that I typed in and found the best match. There’s no intelligence there.”

Avtar remains as sceptical as ever about giving big tech his data, even though it was ChatGPT’s readiness to scrape blogs and give out personal information that led him to his maternal family. Had Avtar chosen to ask another AI, he might not have found Nicci at all. When he came back to Canada, he put the same prompt into Anthropic’s Claude, to see what it would say, just for fun. “It replied, ‘We don’t want to infringe on anybody’s privacy, so we don’t give out that information,” Avtar tells me. Then he shrugs. “I think that’s a good response.”

Empty cupboards to full hearts - Tonga's remarkable road to Glasgow
description: Tonga launch their first Commonwealth Games netball campaign on Saturday in Glasgow when they face Australia, the world's preeminent team. How they got to this stage is remarkable.
fullText:
No team. No coach. No training facilities.

When Salote Sisifa became CEO of Tonga Netball in 2014, she had a blank canvas. Some would call it an empty cupboard.

Twelve years and much upheaval later, the Pacific Islanders are ranked eighth in the world. For context, that's just behind Wales and ahead of Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Tonga launch their first Commonwealth Games netball campaign on Saturday in Glasgow when they face Australia, the world's preeminent team.

Their story is remarkable. It tells of how TV anchor Sisifa went from reading the news to making the news, changing her country's sporting future.

It takes in national crises that include a 2022 volcanic eruption of quite staggering force, the destructive tsunami that followed, and the arrival of Covid-19 - almost two years after most of the world was first hit - to hamper relief efforts.

Sisifa said she would resign if she failed as CEO. She's still firmly at the helm.

Tonga consists of more than 170 islands and is located in the South Pacific.

It is about 2,600 miles from Melbourne, Australia, and its population of 105,000 could almost squeeze into the stands of the famous Melbourne Cricket Ground.

The islands are home to a national netball team who have nailed down a top 10 world ranking for the past four years, but it took a meteoric rise to reach this position.

Sisifa and head coach Jaqua Pori-Makea-Simpson have travelled thousands of miles to recruit players, securing their star shooter thanks to a persuasive grandma.

They still face challenges, with their pathway side - below the senior national squad - having to train in a bank's car park.

When Sisifa signed up, she found netball in Tonga was little more than a social game.

She swiftly committed Tonga to entering a team for the 2015 Pacific Games.

"The scores... we were being beaten like it was a cricket match," she recalls.

More like rugby scorelines perhaps - Tonga lost 88-21 to Samoa, and 81-27 to Papua New Guinea.

Sisifa went to the national governing body for netball in Tonga and said: "Please give me five years. We're going to make some dramatic changes. If it doesn't work within the five years, I would happily resign."

The national body backed Sisifa, so she got to work.

She needed a coach with international pedigree and so wrote to eight candidates. Only one replied.

New Zealand-born Pori-Makea-Simpson joined in 2019.

Sisifa remembers their frank first conversation: "We had no dollar sign to our name. I said if that's what you're looking for, Team Tonga is not the place."

Then came mention of Tonga's vision.

"I said, by 2025, I want Tonga to make top 10 in the world," Sisifa told BBC World Service.

Pori-Makea-Simpson recalls: "I went... you're mad. That is obscene, and I'm not sure you understand what the netball world looks like."

Players with Tongan backgrounds were sought, even if they had never visited the country. This led to some backlash, but Pori-Makea-Simpson felt the players she found shared a culture with islanders.

"Taking them back to Tonga and watching them thrive and grow with their people, it's been beautiful," she said.

The spirit of Tala: The rapid rise of Tonga's netball team

Uneeq Palavi, also known as Pav, has a Samoan mother and Tongan father. She grew up in Australia and has been a Melbourne Mavericks fan favourite.

In 2019, she initially ignored Tonga's call, not feeling ready.

Sisifa roped in Palavi's Tongan grandmother to apply a little persuasion. It worked.

Tonga won silver at the Pacific Games and jumped from 42nd to 19th in the world.

They were moving in the right direction, but then came problem upon problem: a volcanic eruption, tsunami and pandemic lockdown all struck in early 2022.

When the underwater Hunga-Tonga Hunga-Haʻapai erupted, it resulted in the biggest atmospheric explosion recorded by modern instrumentation.

Nasa said it was hundreds of times more powerful than the atomic bomb the US dropped on Hiroshima in 1945.

Four people in Tonga died, and devastation from the eruption and subsequent tsunami was vast. For a while, communication with the island was difficult.

Pori-Makea-Simpson, who was out of the country, had to lead without Tonga Netball's support.

"I had no team, no administration, I didn't have uniforms, I had no equipment," she says.

She had an upcoming PacificAus Sports series and had to draw together a squad almost from scratch, searching social media for eligible players.

Most had never met before they gathered at Sydney Airport five days before competition began.

"I didn't even know their names. They didn't know each other's names. Even when we had finished the tournament, I still didn't know everybody's surnames," Pori-Makea-Simpson recalls.

Against the odds, Tonga won gold.

Star shooter Palavi speaks of a cultural bond.

"Playing for Tonga is always like playing with 15 of my other sisters," she said.

Next came a rare World Cup appearance in 2023, with the team taking on the nickname of Tala - a rare bird that is a symbol of hope.

They finished eighth in South Africa and now comes a Commonwealth Games debut.

Team spirit, and considerable talent, have taken this team a long way.

"I think non-Pacific Island people would call it a camaraderie. It's not a camaraderie. It's an innate spirituality that connects them," says coach Pori-Makea-Simpson.

"In a way that is very, very hard to understand from the outside. You can feel it from the people in the crowd.

"Irrespective of what happens to us in terms of scoreboard, their pride and gratitude to us wearing their crest and their flag will never falter.

"And they're not proud of us because we're winning. They're proud of us because we're Tongan. I am probably the proudest non-Tongan walking on the planet."

title: Joshua v Prenga - heavyweight predictions
description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's heavyweight fight between Anthony Joshua and Kristian Prenga.
fullText:
Anthony Joshua returns to the ring on Saturday against the relatively unknown Kristian Prenga in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, knowing that victory would set up a long-awaited showdown with Tyson Fury.

Joshua, a two-time world champion and Olympic gold medallist, has won 29 fights - 26 by stoppage - and lost four.

Albanian Prenga enters the fight with an impressive record of his own, having achieved all of his 20 victories with stoppages while suffering only one defeat.

However, the 35-year-old has never faced anyone close to Joshua's level.

Joshua v Prenga - all you need to know

After Fury comfortably dispatched Polish veteran Mariusz Wach in Thailand on Friday, can Joshua can come through his own warm-up bout?

This will be Joshua's first fight since he was involved in a car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of two close friends, Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele.

The Fury-Joshua fight has been a decade in the making. Contracts have been signed, with the blockbuster bout expected to take place later this year.

But could Prenga spoil the party and pull off a huge shock to go down in boxing history as the man who got in the way of Joshua-Fury happening?

Radio commentary from Jeddah will begin from about 20:30 BST on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, and the BBC Sport website and app.

Live text commentary will begin at 19:30 on the BBC Sport website and app.

BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for Saturday's fight.

"I think AJ will win by a stoppage late. He has to be careful at the beginning of the fight because a lot of Prenga's stoppages have come in the first couple of rounds - he rarely goes past six rounds, so that's uncharted territory."

"I think AJ will have a look in the first round but it will be over round three or four. I think he'll go right though this guy. I hope he does and we see him and Fury."

Ready to 'conquer Earth' - Joshua embraces comeback spotlight

Joshua v Prenga - all you need to know

"Joshua coming back from what he has is a testament to himself. His attitude and mental resilience. I haven't seen much of Prenga, but I've heard he's a tough guy. If the right Anthony Joshua goes out there and performs, he's a hard night for anyone. If he goes out and performs, he can put anyone on their back. He needs to not overthink. Do your job, get in and get out."

"Obviously it's been an incredibly difficult time for AJ but he seems mentally and physically in a good place, training under Team Usyk.

"I expect him to go out there and emphatically deal with Prenga, who has not fought at anywhere near Joshua's level. So Joshua to win within the first four rounds."

"I think it's a fascinating opponent for AJ to take, because although you may criticise Prenga's style and that it might not look the best, he was a tough unbeaten kickboxer. We saw with Rico Verhoeven against Usyk that these kickboxers can make it tough. I expect AJ to look fresh, establish a quick jab early and have attention to detail.

"He looks very lean, I think he'll be quicker than before and I think he's going to get a clean win. Prenga will try but I think AJ will walk him on to a shot."

"In recent times, you're never quite sure which version of Joshua would turn up on the night.

"But saying that, any version of Joshua will have too much for Prenga. He's big and powerful, but I think he's out of his depth.

"I think Joshua will be a little bit more confident and forceful against this level of opposition. I think it will be three or four rounds before Joshua gets to him with a stoppage."

"You will not see a third round. Joshua will win by a brutal, nasty and vicious knockout."

"I predict a brutal Joshua win, early. It won't go past three rounds. Do not blink."

"AJ will win whenever he wants - it's a run-out for him. Prenga has a flattering record, but if you look at his style, he's pretty cumbersome. Prenga will walk on to shots but AJ's class, his jab and his power punch will have a massive impact. It depends if Joshua wants a few rounds and to practise what he's been doing with his new team.

"It will last as long as Joshua wants it to - maybe four or five rounds."

"AJ will win by knockout between rounds three and five."

"Like most, I'll be honest, I've not seen much of Prenga, but what I have seen, it's a gigantic step up.

"The last 12 to 18 months outside the ring and in with the Dubois defeat being a bad one, Joshua can be excused for this type of opponent.

"With AJ and the power he carries, it could be over in a matter of seconds. I expect him to take his time a little bit and for him to knock Prenga out in three rounds."

title: Sean McCann - brother of Madeleine - to swim at Commonwealths
description: Sean McCann, the younger brother of Madeleine McCann, will swim for Scotland at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Saturday.
fullText:
Sean McCann - the younger brother of Madeleine McCann - will swim for Scotland at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Saturday.

The 21-year-old - a Loughborough University student - is entered in the 400m, 800m and 1500m freestyle events as he makes his debut at a major championships.

The 400m heats begin on Saturday morning at the Tollcross Swimming Centre.

"I'm very excited. It's my first senior Games so I'm just looking forward to representing Scotland and doing my absolute best," McCann told Loughborough University earlier this week, external.

"It's the pinnacle really of representing Scotland at the Commonwealth Games, especially at a home Games.

"I've got lots of family up in Glasgow so that makes it even more special. I was there in 2014 [at the Commonwealth Games], watching as a kid, so to make it now, 12 years later, is really a full-circle moment."

McCann grew up in England but qualifies to compete for Scotland through his father, Gerry.

He and his twin sister were two years old when Madeleine, then aged three, went missing during a family holiday in Praia Da Luz, Portugal, in 2007.

It became one of the world's most high-profile missing-person cases and remains an ongoing Metropolitan Police investigation.

McCann, who balances his swimming with studying for a chemical engineering degree, has been part of the Scottish Swimming programme since his teens.

He finished third in the 800m freestyle and fourth in the 1500m at the British Championships earlier this year.

McCann previously competed at the 2024 Championships, which doubled as Team GB's Olympic trials.

His progression to the senior Commonwealth Games comes after representing Scotland at the 2023 Commonwealth Youth Games in Trinidad and Tobago.

There he finished fifth in the 400m freestyle and seventh in the 1,500m freestyle.

He also raced for Great Britain at the 2025 European Open Water Championships in Croatia.

Speaking about his expectations for Glasgow, he said: "I'm going in as more of an underdog. I don't feel like there's any pressure on me. I should be able to go in and perform at my best."

title: On the move - football's youngest journeymen
description: The players who had appeared for a remarkable number of clubs by their 23rd birthday.
fullText:
Some of football's most celebrated players stayed loyal to a single club for their entire career.

The Premier League's most-decorated player, Ryan Giggs, is one, so too AC Milan legend Paolo Maldini, Roma's Francesco Totti and Arsenal defender Tony Adams.

Perhaps some current players such as Bukayo Saka and Phil Foden might join them too.

But there are players at the other end of the spectrum, those who can look back on a lengthy list of employers, and sometimes while their career is still in its infancy.

The most famous current example is Jhon Duran, the former Aston Villa striker joining the seventh club of his career at the age of just 22 last week.

He joins others who were in danger of acquiring the journeyman tag before their 23rd birthday. These are some of those players.

Dubbed "the next Pele" by some, Freddy Adu was signed by Nike at 13, played Major League Soccer for D.C. United at 14 and made his debut for the United States at 16.

Between 2004 and 2011, he signed for eight different clubs, playing in the US, Portugal, Monaco, Greece and Turkey - and even completed a trial at Manchester United in 2006 - all by the age of 22.

In 2012, Adu spoke of how signing for Benfica in 2007 was "not a good decision".

"As an 18-year-old, there was too much pressure to win right away and I went through three coaches in one year."

Adu, now 37, last played in 2021 for Osterlen FF in Sweden.

In 2010, Croatian goalkeeper Matej Delac signed for Chelsea from Inter Zapresic.

Despite spending eight years at the club, most of his time was spent on loan. By the age of 22, he'd played for eight different clubs - without making a single competitive first-team appearance for the Blues.

Delac, now 33, currently plays for AC Horsens in Denmark.

In 2017, Watford signed 22-year-old Nathaniel Chalobah from Chelsea on a five-year deal.

Although it was the midfielder's first permanent transfer of his career, he had already completed six loan spells (including one with the Hornets in 2012), meaning he had played for a total of seven different clubs by the age of 22.

Chalobah made an impressive start to life at Watford, earning a call-up to the senior England squad for the final round of 2018 World Cup qualifiers. In October 2018, he won his only cap, coming on as a substitute in a 3-2 Uefa Nations League victory over Spain.

Now 31, he's currently without a club having left Sheffield Wednesday following the 2025–26 season.

Josh McEachran was regarded as one of Chelsea's brightest prospects after breaking into the first team as a 17-year-old in 2010, going on to make 22 senior appearances for the club.

He spent the 2014–15 season loaned to Dutch club Vitesse Arnhem after previous loan spells with Swansea, Middlesbrough, Watford and Wigan.

At the age of 22, he signed for Brentford for an undisclosed fee - the seventh club of his career.

At the time of the move, the midfielder spoke about it being time for him "to get out" of Chelsea and how the transfer would give him "stability".

McEachran, 33, spent last season with Bristol Rovers in League Two.

Ryan Bertrand began his professional career at Chelsea and, by the age of 22, had played for six clubs following multiple loan moves

These included two spells each at Bournemouth and Norwich City respectively, as well as loan stints with Oldham Athletic, Reading and Nottingham Forest.

The former England international was loaned out a total of nine separate occasions while at Chelsea before signing permanently for Southampton in 2015, aged 25.

At Chelsea, the left-back made his European debut in the Blues' victory over Bayern Munich in the 2012 final.

Bertrand has been out of the game since leaving Leicester City in 2023.

After beginning his professional career with Dinamo Zagreb at the age of 16, highly rated Croatian midfielder Alen Halilovic earned a permanent move to Barcelona, where he spent two years before joining Hamburg for a further two seasons.

During his time at the Nou Camp, he played primarily for Barcelona B before spending the 2015–16 season on loan at Sporting Gijon.

After joining Hamburg in 2016, he was loaned out to La Liga side Las Palmas during the 2017–18 campaign.

In 2018, shortly after his 22nd birthday, he signed for AC Milan, the sixth club of his career - while Italy became the fourth different country in which he had played.

The midfielder later had spells with Birmingham City and Reading. He now plays for Fortuna Sittard in the Netherlands.

Former Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson once claimed, external that 14-year-old Ravel Morrison was the most talented youngster he had seen at the club since Paul Scholes. However, Morrison's career was hindered by legal issues and disciplinary problems.

He left United, signing for West Ham United in 2012, where he went on to have loan spells with Birmingham City, Queens Park Rangers and Cardiff City.

Before his 23rd birthday, he'd signed for Lazio in Italy - his sixth club in five years.

Reflecting on his career in 2021, the midfielder described West Ham as one of the most "enjoyable" places he played.

However, reports of a disagreement over a contract with then-manager Sam Allardyce brought his time with the Hammers to an end.

The 33-year-old now plays for Arabian Falcons F.C. in the UAE Second Division.

He began his career with Paris St-Germain but left in 1997, saying he was not playing enough and that a lack of first-team opportunities was harming his international prospects.

While at Arsenal, Anelka claimed he was unhappy with the English media, whom he accused of inventing stories about him.

He moved to Real Madrid in 1999 but struggled to settle in Spain and re-signed for PSG in 2000. He returned to the Premier League in 2001, signing on loan for Liverpool aged 22.

In total, the Frenchman played for 12 clubs across seven different countries during his career.

title: 'Maybe he's a racist' - Trump critical of James
description: United States President Donald Trump said LeBron James might be "a racist" when asked if the basketball star is the "best ever" to play the sport.
fullText:
United States President Donald Trump said LeBron James might be "a racist" when asked if the basketball star is the "best ever" to play the sport.

James, 41, announced on Friday he is set to continue his glittering career with the Philadelphia 76ers.

When asked about the move in a White House news conference later, Trump explained why he believed Michael Jordan was the better player.

Jordan, 63, won six NBA titles with the Chicago Bulls in the 1990s and NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP) five times.

When asked whether Jordan or James was the "best ever", Trump said: "Michael Jordan is a guy that's a friend of mine. I play golf with him. He's a really good guy.

"I think LeBron is, maybe he's a racist, but maybe he doesn't like Trump. I don't know. I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way."

James, who has not responded to Trump's comment, has been a regular critic of Trump during his terms as president and endorsed Democrat candidates Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris when they ran against him.

In 2017 he referred to Trump as "a bum" following a row over invitations to the White House for NBA-winning teams.

James has won four NBA titles with the Miami Heat (twice), the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Los Angeles Lakers.

He has been named the league's MVP four times and is the NBA's all-time leader in points and games played.

James will be looking to secure a fifth title with the 76ers following his announcement on Friday that he is heading to Philadelphia.

They now boast the talents of James and All-Stars Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team," James said in a lengthy post on social media.

title: USA's Lyles wins 100m in world-leading 9.79 seconds
description: Noah Lyles runs a world-leading 9.79 seconds as he claims an impressive victory in the 100m at the US athletics championships.
fullText:
Noah Lyles ran a world-leading 9.79 seconds as he claimed an impressive victory in the 100m at the US athletics championships.

He also equalled his personal best, which he set in winning gold at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, with the run at the Icahn Stadium in New York City.

The previous best 100m in 2026 was the 9.82 set by Jamaica's Oblique Seville in June.

"I think I made that 'I'm still the world's fastest man' statement," said Lyles.

The 29-year-old American finished ahead of Ronnie Baker in second and third-placed Kenny Bednarek, who were both given a time of 9.88, while former world champion Christian Coleman was fourth in 9.93.

"Just because it is an off year doesn't mean that I plan to run slow," added Lyles, referring to there being no Olympics or World Championships this year.

"This is me being me and being me is dominant, being consistent."

Sha'Carri Richardson, the 2023 world champion, won the women's 100m as she clocked 10.77.

The 26-year-old equalled her best time of the season as Kayla White finished second with 10.90 and Tamari Davis third in 11.00.

"It just feels phenomenal to be back in a better place, just healthy mentally, physically and emotionally," said Richardson, who has had troubles off the track.

"Everything me and coach have been working on, it's starting to show consistently."

title: How do Manchester City manage the Rodri dilemma?
description: BBC Sport looks at what City's new-look midfield could be like and whether it is time to cash in on Rodri.
fullText:
Replacing a manager after 10 years is no easy feat, let alone when there appears to be a squad overhaul too.

Four of the starters in City's Treble-winning side of 2022-23 - Manuel Akanji, Nathan Ake, Bernardo Silva and John Stones - have left this summer, with the Blues signing £116m Elliot Anderson and promising 17-year-old Jeremy Monga.

And the changes might not end there.

Fresh from captaining Spain to World Cup victory, Rodri will head for back surgery on Monday with just a year left on his contract, amid increasing speculation about his future.

It is not clear how long the 30-year-old will spend on the sidelines, but one thing new boss Enzo Maresca was clear on in his first news conference was that he wants to keep him.

But with reports that Real Madrid are "operating on the basis" of Rodri joining them,, external what do City do?

Will they look to cash in when Rodri returns to fitness, or keep to Maresca's stance?

And how might Maresca's midfield operate - with or without Rodri?

When Rodri returned from an anterior cruciate ligament injury last year, there will have been plenty who wondered whether he would return to the Ballon d'Or-winning levels he had reached at his peak.

Pep Guardiola - the man Maresca has replaced - said last October: "In the World Cup, he will be the best Rodri, and next season he will be the best Rodri."

Guardiola was proved right on the first count. Not only did Rodri captain Spain to World Cup success but he was also awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.

Maresca was unequivocal when asked for his view on Friday.

"I think every manager wants to have Rodri because he is a top player," he said.

"But now, surgery on Monday... he needs a holiday... he needs to rest and recover and then he will be back with us."

The plan seems clear, therefore - look to retain one of the best players in world football rather than sell him.

But there will have to be contingencies in place.

One of these will be the presence of Anderson, while City are monitoring 18-year-old Lille midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi, who impressed for Morocco in the World Cup.

To understand how Rodri, Anderson and someone like Bouaddi might come together, it is key to understand Maresca's game model.

As a disciple of positional play, he draws comparisons between his football and chess.

"There are a lot of similarities," Maresca said. "The most important is positional play and strategy.

"For a coach, it's important to have the mentality of a chess player: develop a plan, study counter-moves, choose the arrangement of the pieces."

Maresca's strategy has largely been rooted in an on-the-ball shape that looks like a 3-2-2-3.

One of Rodri's most useful qualities in a Maresca side would be his ability to move between these predefined positions on the pitch.

Throughout the World Cup, for example, we saw him drop into the backline when former City team-mate Aymeric Laporte pushed up with the ball.

Naturally, Rodri spent most of the game in a holding midfield position, but when space opened up he was more than capable of pushing forward too.

At their best, Maresca's sides use rotations of players within the 3-2-2-3. His innovation often comes in the form of creating this shape in new ways.

Defending as a 4-4-2 before attacking in the 3-2-2-3, it was Stones who stepped up from centre-back into a midfield pair with Rodri during City's Treble-winning season, when Maresca was assistant manager.

At Chelsea, one of Maresca's more unique tweaks involved playing Moises Caicedo at right-back. Defending with a back four before again attacking in a 3-2-2-3 shape, Caicedo would move from right-back into one of the holding midfield positions.

Here is where the signing of Anderson makes such sense.

Throughout his career, the 23-year-old has played in every midfield and attacking position at one point. For England, he has frequently dropped into defence to form a back five out of possession.

Alongside Rodri, Anderson would be able to sit deep, allowing the Spaniard to showcase his attacking quality - and vice versa.

Both players would be capable of taking turns in dropping deeper to maintain the balance of the team if strong carriers of the ball like Marc Guehi or Josko Gvardiol were to push forward.

Piggy-backing on the success of Rodri's work with Bernardo Silva, City would hope their new versatile and combative winger-turned-holding-midfielder will bring about similar success.

Bouaddi - like Anderson - has played in a number of roles, more specifically holding midfield, right-back and centre-back.

His ability to occupy those positions - with strong defending and elegance on the ball - replicates some of the work Stones did for City.

The club are looking at young and intelligent footballers capable of playing for possession-heavy sides. More important, however, is their ability to be positionally versatile across the roles Maresca's system demands.

When numerous players can move into any of the positions that open up, it can result in a structured yet fluid team that become harder for the opposition to defend against – think Luis Enrique's Paris St-Germain.

But this takes both time and tutelage.

City will look better with Rodri, who possesses an understanding of positioning, speed and risk that Anderson and future signings may take time to grasp.

After all, it took Rodri a few seasons to navigate the change in environment under Fernandinho's wing.

But should he go, Maresca has previously shown an impressive ability to recognise positions players could move into but haven't yet done: Stones into holding midfield, Caicedo into full-back, Marc Cucurella into attacking midfield... the list goes on.

Whether or not City further bolster their squad, Maresca will hope to have a greater number of pieces to place on his board - a departure from Guardiola's approach of maintaining a smaller squad.

That factor - and this holds true whether or not Rodri stays - should give City's new boss a greater chance of landing on a working formula next season.
