title: IBM Acquiring HRL Laboratories
description: IBM announced it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire HRL Laboratories, LLC (HRL), a flagship research and development institution.
fullText:
ARMONK, NY and MALIBU, CA, July 23, 2026 -- IBM (NYSE: IBM) today announced it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire HRL Laboratories, LLC (HRL), a flagship research and development institution. HRL is a private company jointly owned by Boeing and General Motors.  Both Boeing and GM will continue to partner with IBM on quantum applications and advanced technology development following the transaction.

HRL's advanced expertise in silicon-spin qubit engineering will complement and extend IBM’s long-term mission to scale increasingly powerful quantum computers and accelerate its quantum vision.  Superconducting qubits and spin qubits both leverage state-of-the art silicon fabrication. This shared foundation is amongst the reasons why these two modalities offer credible paths to scaling quantum technologies.

“The HRL team will help IBM push even farther forward toward the frontiers of quantum innovation,” said Jay Gambetta, IBM’s Director of Research and IBM Fellow. “This talented group of researchers brings a broad portfolio of technologies that will strengthen IBM's long-term plans to deliver useful quantum computing to the world, bringing together advances across quantum computing, quantum sensing, and quantum networking to enable the applications of the future.”

“Joining IBM is the natural next chapter for what we have built at HRL, where our team has dedicated years to exploring paths to how future quantum computers could be built at scales that today seem impossible,” said Rob Vasquez, President and Chief Executive Officer at HRL “We now look forward to leveraging IBM’s industry leadership and working alongside their world-class talent on fundamental infrastructure to take this vision forward. Additionally, our cutting-edge physical and information science innovations will combine with their advanced research capabilities to deliver an unmatched suite of technology solutions for our commercial and government customers.”

HRL will also enable IBM to innovate in and industrialize promising technologies such as quantum sensing and drive new research into quantum materials. This includes ultra precise quantum sensors capable of detecting subtle physical phenomena and capturing finely tuned measurements for life sciences, navigation, defense, and scientific applications. Combined with additional capabilities in cryogenics, control electronics, qubit interconnects, and packaging, IBM anticipates that HRL’s technical breakthroughs will help fuel its quantum program for decades to come.

Additionally, HRL has developed innovations in novel quantum materials that have the potential to unlock better semiconductors and more sensitive sensors – all of which can optimize the performance and scalability of a wide range of quantum technologies.

Beyond its leadership in quantum computing, HRL brings deep expertise in advanced sensors, high-speed and high-power communications, electronics, advanced manufacturing, and materials science, developed through decades of research and development for both commercial and U.S. government customers. HRL’s broad technology portfolio will complement IBM’s innovation leadership and help accelerate the development of next-generation computing, communications, and mission-critical systems.

Advancing Quantum Computers for Generations to Come

IBM continues to define the direction for the industry with superconducting qubit-based architectures, including breakthroughs in error correction and new algorithms enabling quantum computers to run harder problems more efficiently. IBM's roadmap to deliver the world's first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers is clear and on course. This includes delivering IBM Quantum Starling by 2029, which will be 20,000 times more powerful than today’s quantum computers and capable of running 100 million quantum operations. In the mid-2030s, Starling will be followed by the even more powerful Blue Jay quantum computer, projected to be capable of 1 billion quantum operations.

As IBM looks to further extend quantum computing, HRL will bring robust knowledge of silicon‑based spin qubit platforms and surrounding infrastructure that could offer new insights into how to best scale quantum computers into the next decade.

In May 2026, IBM further expanded its global quantum leadership when the company announced it would establish Anderon, the world’s first pure-play quantum wafer foundry. As a standalone IBM company, Anderon is being created with the support of the U.S. Department of Commerce to enable scalable, consistent, and agile manufacturing for a broad range of quantum computing modalities and companies. The acquisition of HRL offers an opportunity to partner even more closely with Anderon, including potential plans to develop spin qubit manufacturing to scale quantum manufacturing and enable faster learning cycles.

Financial details of the transaction were not disclosed, and IBM's acquisition of HRL is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. The transaction is anticipated to close by the end of the third quarter of 2026.

title: SpaceX launches Starship on successful test flight
description: Starship demonstrated key abilities on its path to becoming a fully reusable transport for astronauts to the moon
fullText:
SpaceX launches Starship on successful test flight

Starship demonstrated key abilities on its path to becoming a fully reusable transport for astronauts to the moon

Join Our Community of Science Lovers!

SpaceX on Thursday pulled off its second consecutive successful test flight of its Starship megarocket. The launch hints at sustained progress after years of botched tests, but there is a caveat.

Just after 6:50 p.m. Eastern, Starship lofted into space atop SpaceX’s Super Heavy V3 booster from the company’s Starbase launch complex in Boca Chica, Texas. After two-and-a-half minutes, the booster separated from Starship, returning to Earth. SpaceX was aiming for the reusable booster to make a pinpoint landing in the Gulf of Mexico, but that part of the mission didn't go according to plan. The booster’s landing burn appeared to fail, resulting in a spectacular explosion as it hit the water.

Once in space, however, Starship successfully deployed its payload of 20 Starlink V3 satellites, some of which were armed with cameras to check its heat shield—and offer audiences on the ground in-flight views of the rocket in space.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The Starlink satellites are the same as those SpaceX is planning to use to further build out its orbital broadband internet constellation. But for the purposes of this test, the Starlink craft merely attempted to establish laser communications with the wider network, before ultimately plummeting to their doom in Earth’s atmosphere.

Eventually, SpaceX wants to use Starship as its workhorse rocket, replacing the smaller Falcon 9. Starship, able to carry 100 tons of cargo to orbit, will be able to loft many more Starlink at a time than the Falcon 9.

Alone in space, Starship also showed improvements over its last test flight, successfully reigniting one of its six Raptor engines for a brief burn. The spacecraft didn’t attempt this feat during its previous test flight in May, because the Raptor engine shut down prematurely during launch.

The flight, which was originally slated for last week but was delayed, ended after an hour and five minutes. After deploying its satellites, Starship splashed down successfully in the Indian Ocean north of Australia, although it did briefly catch fire in the water.

The mostly successful test is good news for SpaceX’s ambitions—but it also matters for the future of human space exploration. NASA hopes to use Starship to get humans to and from the moon as part of its Artemis program.

If SpaceX can get a lunar-lander variant of Starship ready on time, NASA could use it to send humans to the surface of the moon for the first time in more than 50 years as soon as 2028.

A watchdog report published in March found SpaceX is lagging on that effort, and the space agency is also funding development of a Blue Origin lunar lander for the task.

The clock is ticking for both companies: NASA’s Artemis III, a crewed mission to test key capabilities for both vehicles in low-Earth orbit, is targeted for launch before the end of next year. The current plan is to try to dock NASA’s crew capsule, Orion, with Starship—but SpaceX still needs to show it can get Starship to orbit in the first place. That means many more test flights, if nothing else.

US regulators on Thursday said they plan to develop rules to address the safety risks linked to the hidden electric car door handles popularized by Tesla.

Investigations from Bloomberg have uncovered more than a dozen deaths from crashes in which people became trapped inside a Tesla because the doors wouldn’t open. The EV giant said it is working on a redesign.

China earlier this year became the first country to ban the modern handles, in a move analysts said could influence norms around the world and cement China’s status as a global “rule-setter” for new vehicle tech. Beijing’s ban takes effect next year; safety advocates don’t expect a US rule to come into force before 2030.

title: Protecting War Criminals Is As American as Apple Pie
description: Elie...
fullText:
In this week’s Elie v. US, our justice correspondent bemoans our long failure to prosecute war criminals. Plus: the death of Nolan wells and the nightmare so many Black parents fear.

New Jersey made a mistake. Well, more accurately, software used by New Jersey’s Department of Motor Vehicles made a mistake. The state learned this week that a computer malfunction at the DMV led to approximately 6,600 individuals who indicated that they were not US citizens being registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. Around 400 of these people who were registered incorrectly voted in a New Jersey election.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill apologized for the error, which occurred before she was in office. She released a statement expressing how seriously she takes the problem and assuring the public that the glitch has been fixed and the registrations revoked.

You can imagine how this all went over with the Trump administration. Even before this revelation, the Republican National Committee was working to subpoena voter registration records in New Jersey as part of their endless fishing expedition for alleged voter fraud. That request was soundly rejected in court. But we can expect the RNC to try again based on this DMV error.

And they’ll be joined by the Trump Department of Justice. The DOJ has now requested the full names, addresses, and voter information of the noncitizens incorrectly registered in New Jersey. There’s no reason for the DOJ to have this data; if anything, the DOJ should be investigating the software company that produced the error, not harassing the people who answered truthfully and were accidently registered anyway.

But something worse than harassment will probably happen to the nearly 400 noncitizens who voted. The DOJ will come down on them like a hammer and, most likely, attempt to detain and deport them.

Since nobody in power in the Democratic Party will have the courage to say this, I will stand on a hill and shout that 400 people voting illegally doesn’t matter. Approximately 6,600 people accidentally being registered doesn’t matter.

New Jersey has 6,682,699 registered voters. The DMV error meant that 0.0988 percent of those voters shouldn’t have been registered. In the 2024 presidential election, 4,272,725 people cast a ballot in New Jersey. If 400 people did vote illegally, that works out to 0.00936 percent of total ballots cast.

This error is negligible. It had no effect—and unlike Governor Sherrill, I don’t take it seriously. Caring about this is like caring that somebody is going (pulls out the calculator) 55.005148 miles per hour in a 55mph zone. This entire “issue” is stupid.

Books & the Arts

 /

 Christian Lorentzen

One of the reasons I have little hope that Miller or any of Trump’s odious henchmen will ever face accountability for their fascist actions is that law professor John Yoo is still out there, free and spreading evil. This is the guy who wrote the torture memos during the George W. Bush administration. He’s literally the legal architect of war crimes. And yet, he’s still a “respected” law professor, at Berkeley no less, who regularly goes on television and is allowed to live a life of freedom, despite being the guy who gave Dick Cheney the legal cover for waterboarding. Justice never comes for these people.

Yoo is back in the news because he has the ear of the current administration, and he’s arguing for lawfare against the guy who scares Republicans the most: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the UN General Assembly this fall, Mamdani said he’d “look into” what his options were to arrest the man. Netanyahu is on the lam from the International Criminal Court, which has issued a warrant for his arrest. Mamdani said he’d ask his lawyers if there is anything he can do about that.

He could have asked me (though I’d like to think I’ve priced myself out of a city government salary). The answer is “no.” Netanyahu is protected by diplomatic immunity while traveling to the United Nations. Mamdani literally can’t even give him a parking ticket. And that [deep existential sigh] is as it should be. Leaders from all over the world must be able to travel freely to the UN for the UN to function, and those leaders include strongmen and dictators and people some countries perceive as “evil.” Diplomatic immunity must exist, and must be respected. New Yorkers are not uncivilized thugs like the Spartans.

There’s also a law, the American Service-Members’ Protection Act, that prevents Mamdani from doing anything. This is a Bush era law that prevents US officials from working with the International Criminal Court in any capacity. The Bush regime was particularly interested in not being held accountable for war crimes.

That’s the law Yoo invoked on Fox News while declaring that Mamdani should be investigated by the Justice Department. But, as Joe Patrice explained at Above the Law, Yoo overplayed his hand. You can’t investigate a guy for talking to a lawyer. You can’t charge a guy for breaking the law when he hasn’t broken it. Mamdani called around, asked a few experts; they ultimately told him that Netanyahu is untouchable, and—as Mamdani acknowledged—that’s that. Yoo’s attempt to threaten Mamdani is just another case of MAGA trying to gin up some reason to go after the popular lefty mayor.

The American Service-Members’ Protection Act is, by the way, a shit law. It’s something that either Obama or Biden should have repealed the first chance they got. It’s sometimes called the “Hague Invasion Act” because it preposterously argues that the United States can send military forces to the Hague to stage a prison break should one of our people be held there for, let’s not forget, war crimes or crimes against humanity. Any American president should be willing to abide by the rules of the International Criminal Court, and the fact that none of them do—not Republican presidents nor Democratic presidents—is a stain on our country and one of the (many) reasons we’re viewed as global thugs.

Anyway, neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor John Yoo should be able to travel to any country that respects international law. Fortunately for both of them, our country protects war criminals.

I didn’t put anything on the board this week, but, in fairness to me, it’s the middle of the summer, and my kids are done with camp. Also, Jay Willis on Balls and Strikes wrote everything I was going to say about the Supreme Court’s declining poll numbers.

In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos

I haven’t written about the Nolan Wells situation. Wells was an 18-year-old college football player who disappeared over Fourth of July weekend after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, off the Mississippi Gulf coast. Wells and a bunch of friends went out, but Wells never came back. His body was found six days later. Mississippi officials have not released the autopsy, although the family ordered a private autopsy that came back inconclusive as to the cause of death.

I haven’t written about it because, even though Wells’s family has hired high-powered lawyer Benjamin Crump, there’s nothing for me to say about the legal, or potentially criminal, circumstances surrounding his death. We don’t know how he died, we don’t know why he died, and while the Mississippi officials appear incredibly unconcerned about his death, there’s not as of yet a cause of action against the state that I can see.

I can only speak about Wells as a parent, and the Wells situation strikes at an acute fear I think is shared, in full, only by other Black parents. Wells happens to be Black, but most of the friends he went on the trip with are white. I can tell you that sending your Black child to any kind of party with predominantly white friends is its own special kind of terror.

You’re not worried that the white friends are going to kill or lynch your child, not exactly anyway. You’re more worried that, should others decide it’s time for a lynching, the white friends will be of no help. You’re not exactly worried that the white friends are going to do something; you’re worried that they won’t do anything when something needs to be done. You’re worried that, in an all-white crowd, your kid is alone, even if the kid thinks they’re with a bunch of friends.

Wells’s white friends all claim that they have no idea what happened to him. I believe them. I have no reason not to believe them. But that’s kind of the point: a whole group of friends, and nobody knows what happened to the Black one. A whole group of buddies, and nobody was looking out for the Black one—on an island in Mississippi, of all places.

And don’t even get me started on how this situation would play out if the races were reversed. If a bunch of Black kids with one white friend went out to an island, and the white one didn’t come home, the Black kids would be under the jail until somebody “remembered” something.

In college, I had a couple of white friends I could trust. On campus, it was whatever, but if we ever went into Boston, they wouldn’t leave me. They knew they couldn’t leave me. They couldn’t let me be the lone Black guy trying to drunkenly get home on the train out of Southie. They had to be around to hail the cab I couldn’t otherwise get.

I survived college. And I’m still friends with them to this day. When I watch my children interact with their white friends in and around school… this is literally the only quality I’m looking for.

fullText:
If you’re not into the futuristic look of Nothing’s over-ear headphones, the brand’s wireless noise-canceling earbuds might be up your alley instead. A more premium update to Nothing’s earlier Ear earbuds, these come with an upgraded charging case and are a solid choice for those who like their earbuds with a side of bass—especially since the Nothing Ear (3) wireless earbuds are now on sale for $129 (originally $149).

The earbuds are comfortable to wear and feature more metal beneath their transparent plastic than their predecessors, giving them an even more polished, high-tech look. Users can pinch the stems to control them rather than pressing buttons: A single pinch plays or pauses audio and answers or ends a phone call, while double and triple pinches skip forward and back, respectively.

The deep bass response comes courtesy of 12mm dynamic drivers with a frequency response of 20Hz to 40kHz. Sound is more sculpted than on previous models and, in Nothing’s Balanced mode, delivers deep, powerful bass. For those using a Nothing phone, pairing the buds gives you the option to interact with ChatGPT through voice commands. The earbuds are rated IP54, making them suitable for workouts and light rain. The case carries the same rating, which is rare.

While battery life is slightly improved from the previous generation, it still leaves something to be desired, with up to 5.5 hours of continuous playback with ANC turned on and up to 22 hours combined with the case. Fast charging can provide up to 10 hours of playback with just 10 minutes of charging. ANC is satisfactory, blocking out up to 45 dB, but falls short of some similarly priced earbuds, according to PCMag.

If your main priority is a cool, stylish aesthetic with a comfortable fit, adequate noise cancellation, and robust, bassy sound, the Nothing Ear (3) wireless earbuds are a great pick, as long as you don't need ultra-long battery life without the case. If you are open to a less stylish option but want best-in-class ANC, the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro earbuds may be a better, albeit pricier, choice.

title: Why Athletes Need Sugar and Carbs in Their Diet
description: The benefits of carbohydrates are often overlooked.
fullText:
Do you have a sense that avoiding carbs is eating “clean?" Do you figure that anything with bread or flour in it is junk food? Is sugar something to be avoided at all costs? If so, we need to have an intervention. Carbs—including sugar—are good, actually. And avoiding them can do more harm than good when it comes to health and fitness.

To find out how much carbohydrate you're actually getting, any nutrition app (like Cronometer, which is free) can keep track of how many grams of carbs you get throughout the day. If you use an AI-based tool, like the chatbots built into many wearable apps these days, make sure to double-check against the food's actual label to be sure it's tracking the grams of carbs correctly.

As I’ve often said, the things we do to lose weight are not the same as things that make us healthier. You can lose weight on a low-carb diet, and that’s fine. But that doesn’t mean that avoiding carbs is going to make you healthier in general.

And in fact, a lot of the downsides of dieting can be improved by allowing yourself more carbs. The fact that low-carb and higher-carb diets can both work for weight loss does not mean that they are equivalent in every way. People who eat more carbs tend to have less fatigue during exercise and get to be more flexible in their diet, whether they are trying to lose weight or not.

Before we get deeper into this subject, let’s talk about what carbs are. Pretty much everything we eat can be categorized as a fat (including oil), a protein, or a carbohydrate. Carbohydrates, or carbs, include:

Sugars, including table sugar, glucose, and fructose. There are naturally occurring sugars in fruits, vegetables, and milk.

Starches, which plants use as a form of carbohydrate storage. White bread and white rice are examples of foods that contain a lot of starch without much else.

Fiber, which our bodies can’t completely digest. Different types of fibers are found in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and beans.

You may hear about “complex” carbs. To a biochemist, starches and fiber are both complex carbs. But the term has been misused to mean “foods with fiber in them,” like fruits and whole grains. White bread is full of complex carbs, so don’t take this distinction too literally.

What’s important to remember is that sugars and starches can both be broken down to create energy for our body fairly quickly. Fiber slows down this process, but so do fats and protein. So if you need fast energy when you’re in the middle of a run, you may prefer sugars or starches. If you want a full meal that you can digest over time, giving you all its various healthy benefits, foods with fiber, protein, and fats will be good for you—but these meals can include sugars and starches in the mix as well.

It’s not great to get a lot of added sugar in your diet; that much is true. And most Americans do get a lot of added sugar in our diet, far more than our bodies can put to good use. I’m not endorsing that excess. (Most of us would probably be better off if we cut out at least some of that sugar.)

But I am saying that we need to pay attention to why too much sugar is bad, and not overreact by demonizing sugar or saying it’s poison, it’s toxic, and that it needs to be eliminated. There’s absolutely no reason to believe those myths. Too much sugar is bad for us because sugar is a dense source of “empty” calories. But our bodies can deal with a moderate amount of sugar just fine.

And if you’re an athlete—even a recreational one, somebody who likes to jog and lift—you may find that simple carbs like sugar help to fuel your workouts. That, in turn, lets you do more quality exercise. Take marathoners as an example: sucking down packet after packet of sugary gels is not natural or normal; but neither is running 26.2 miles at a steady pace without stopping. The one fuels the other. Even if you want to make an argument about what humans evolved to do, you’ll need to come to terms with the fact that hunter-gatherers eat a lot of honey.

If you’ve ever felt pooped during a long workout, you might chalk that up to the workout itself. But people who are either dieting or who are choosing to eat “clean” may feel this way because they’re short on carbs.

I say this based partly on research that has shown fueling to make a huge difference for endurance athletes, as in my example above about marathoners. That much is scientifically established.

The other part is a mostly anecdotal, but strongly supported-by-anecdote observation, that people who eat carbs before their workout tend to feel more energetic in those workouts. It’s why the best stim-free preworkout, if you want to avoid caffeine, is called eating a damn snack. If you’ve been doing fasted cardio, or you’ve been eating keto all day long and then trying to grit your teeth through a workout when you’re exhausted, try having some carbs before your workout. You’ll feel a world of difference.

And it’s not just physical performance. Research also shows that eating a low-carb diet can interfere with cognitive tasks like memory and attention. Your body can get by on a low-carb diet, but it performs best when it has carbs available.

A big part of the reason low-carb diets are effective for weight loss is that it’s hard to avoid carbs when you’re eating out, or grabbing a quick snack on the road. Most processed food products include carbs, but so do most home-cooked meals, unless you’re specifically preparing them without carbs.

As a result, you don’t have much to eat when you’re following a strict low-carb diet, and that’s a big part of why it becomes so easy to limit your calories. But notice that if you’ve cut out carbs, you’ll end up avoiding a lot of healthy foods, including fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, which have plenty of vitamins and other nutrients that need to be present in a healthy diet. It’s real hard to eat fiber if you’re swearing off starches and sugars as well.

It’s important to get enough protein, and I don’t just mean hitting the bare minimum of the RDA. If you work out, you’ll want more protein, and if you’re trying to lose weight, you’ll want even more protein, to name a few common reasons why it’s good to work protein into your diet.

Carbohydrates actually help you with this job. Carbs are understood to be “protein-sparing,” meaning that if you get plenty of carbs in your diet, your body is less interested in breaking protein down to burn it for energy. Or to put it another way: on a low-carb diet, some of the protein you eat goes to waste, just because your body needs some kind of fuel for energy, and it doesn’t have its preferred source, carbs. So if you have a hard time getting enough protein in your diet, making sure that you have plenty of carbs will help the protein you do get to go farther.

title: Instagram Is Starting to Crack Down on Creepy Smart Glasses Videos
description: Creepy videos are being more heavily scrutinized by Meta.
fullText:
In a recent story posted on Instagram, Instagram head Adam Mosseri revealed the social media platform is banning smart glasses videos where people are being harassed and exploited for views.

"If you're posting content that is taking advantage of people and harassing them, like a lot of these pickup line kind of videos that we've heard of and seen, then we're going to take the content down," Mosseri said. "We don't want people to be surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform. So we're trying to fight that every way we can."

Hidden camera prank videos and "pickup" type videos are obviously not new, but the easy availability of camera glasses has led to a spike in this kind of content, with videos of men trying to pick up women, pranking retail workers, and other pranks appearing more frequently across all video-sharing services.

Business Insider reported that Meta recently pulled two accounts with over a million followers for posting "pickup artist" videos, where women who may not have known they were being filmed have their videos posted online, leading to harassment. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that the accounts were nuked in accordance with the company's existing bullying and harassment policy.

Meta's official policy on bullying states "We remove content that's meant to degrade or shame, including, for example, claims about someone's sexual activity," and lists a number of specific examples like, "severe sexualized commentary" and "calls for, or statements of intent to engage in, bullying and/or harassment." But there's a lot of gray area. Videos featuring vaguely aggressive acts directed at strangers apparently aren't in violation of Meta's standards, for instance. Neither is a video like the one below, but I'd feel pretty harassed if I were that doctor.

There isn't a reliable way to automate harassment detection because so much of what constitutes harassment comes down to intent and context. This leaves enforcement up to users who can flag videos and/or victims, who are often unaware their image is being spread online until it's too late to put the toothpaste back in the tube.

The backlash over camera-equipped smart glasses is definitely growing, whether its apps designed to suss them out in public, condemnation from pop stars, or outright bans on smart glasses in some places.

As a privacy safeguard, Meta's glasses have a front-facing light that comes on when video is being taken or a picture is being snapped, but the light has been an ongoing issue since the glasses launched. Disabling it has turned into an ongoing game of cat-and-mouse: Meta smart glasses' cameras won't work if the light is covered, but hackers found ways to modify the hardware itself, leading Meta to release a mandatory update that will physically disable any glasses if a user tampers with the indicator. Creeps are pretty ingenious, so I expect further workarounds.

Whether they have lights or not, hidden cameras are generally legal to use in public places in the U.S. (with a few exceptions), and it's not necessarily against the law to film yourself trying to pick someone up, then post the footage online so weirdos can comment, either.

Unless you're really eagle-eyed, it's tough to spot someone with a hacked pair of glasses with no recording indicator light, but it's not impossible. Here are a few things to look for:

The rivet: Most standard glasses have decoration of some kind to cover the glasses' hinge. On Meta Ray-Bans and most other camera glasses, they're round and slightly oversized with a glass inner circle.

Thick frames: While the technology is getting smaller, camera equipped glasses tend to have thicker frames to hide the gear.

The tap: There's two ways to trigger an off-the-shelf pair of Meta smart glasses, saying "Hey, Meta, take video" or tapping the side of the glasses.

Head movement: Meta glasses have a pretty wide lens, so they don't require a ton of movement to capture a scene, but still, if someone is moving their head when they could just be moving their eyes, they might be trying to keep something in frame.

All that said, despite the growing popularity of the nickname "pervert glasses," camera-equipped smart glasses have a variety of legitimate uses and I assume the vast majority of wearers want a quick way to upload content to Instagram, answer texts, or take a picture without having to pull out their phones, so just spotting the glasses in the wild doesn't mean you've spotted a creeper. Usually.

title: Man Utd mascot, six, hit by club's ticket tout crackdown
description: Ruari's mum denies any wrongdoing and says she manages other family members' tickets for them.
fullText:
A mother has said her six-year-old son has had restrictions put on his Manchester United season ticket as part of the club's anti-touting crackdown.

Katie, 39, from Urmston, Trafford, said she had been left unable to apply for an away game ticket for her "football daft" son Ruari - who had once been a match mascot - ahead of the Premier League opener against Hull.

In an email seen by the BBC, the club said repeated access to Ruairi's account, alongside an "extremely high" number of other ticketing accounts, indicated they had been centrally controlled.

But Katie - who said her appeal to the club had been turned down - said she had just helped other family members to use their accounts and had done nothing wrong.

Ruari is among "thousands" of fans who have had their accounts restricted by the club in a wider operation aimed at identifying potential ticket touts.

Man Utd previously said it was confident the "vast majority" of accounts identified for misuse had been correctly flagged, but acknowledged some supporters who were doing nothing wrong might also have been affected.

Katie said she had lodged a further appeal with the club's appeals panel, but Ruari's account remains restricted.

Katie said Ruairi had held a season ticket since birth and regularly attended home, away and European matches with his family.

Supporting Man Utd was "all we do", she said, adding that she met her husband at Old Trafford and had held her own season ticket for nearly 20 years, along with her late mother and siblings.

"Since [Ruari] could walk, he's had a ball at his feet," she said. "He's just football daft."

Katie said Ruairi had been a United mascot at Crystal Palace last season and had travelled to watch the team in Seville, Istanbul and Bilbao.

A post on X, in which Katie said the restriction would "break [Ruari's] heart", has been viewed more than 1.3 million times.

She said she had not told him about the restriction because "you can't put that on a six-year-old".

"The first game of the season, we're definitely going to miss," she said.

"I looked at his dad and said, 'How can you take that away from him?'"

Katie said 19 relatives and friends had formed a group so they could sit together in a singing section at Old Trafford.

She said she handled much of their ticket administration, including away applications, while family members helped one another manage accounts using shared devices and internet connections.

Some relatives were less confident using online ticketing systems, she said.

Katie's appeal challenges restrictions on six family accounts.

In it, she said no tickets had been sold for profit, advertised or supplied to unauthorised third parties, and no automated software, bots or scripts had been used.

She said that when family members had been unable to attend one or two matches, their tickets had been forwarded through Man Utd's official system.

The club's decision email said applying with other supporters and using its official forwarding process had not, by itself, been treated as evidence of wrongdoing.

However, it said the "scale, frequency and pattern" of the wider activity had not been satisfactorily explained.

The club concluded that Ruairi's account and its associated tickets had been put under another person's control and used or managed outside its authorised processes.

The email did not expressly accuse the family of reselling tickets or using bots.

Man Utd told Katie on the afternoon of 21 July that the restriction would remain, about four hours after she first sent her explanation.

The email said the decision followed a "detailed review" of the information she provided and the club's investigation.

Katie said she believed it was an "AI automated rejection" because it arrived so quickly and appeared to use the same wording as responses received by other supporters.

Man Utd declined to comment on Ruari's case.

But the club said similar anti-touting work last season recovered more than 14,000 tickets worth more than £1m and returned them to supporters through official channels.

title: LA Dodgers and MVP Ohtani launch summer of live baseball on BBC
description: World Series champions the Los Angeles Dodgers will launch a summer of live Major League Baseball on the BBC.
fullText:
Defending World Series champions the Los Angeles Dodgers will launch a summer of live Major League Baseball on the BBC when they meet the New York Mets on Sunday.

The Dodgers lead the National League again in 2026, with last season's Most Valuable Player, Shohei Ohtani, to the fore as they target a third consecutive World Series title.

The struggling Mets are in need of inspiration from star man Juan Soto as they look to turn around a difficult start to the season.

The game sets up a run of 10 consecutive live Sunday night MLB matches on the BBC, including the season finale on September 27 before four post-season games the following week.

Why Dodgers are on brink of World Series dynasty

The night the Tartan Army took over iconic Fenway Park

The Dodgers' record of 65 wins and 38 defeats means they are likely to win the National League West for the 13th time in 14th years.

Their recent dominance is built around Ohtani, whose achievements are now compared to the greatest players in the history of the game.

His ability to both hit and pitch at the top level consistently - he already has 22 home runs this year and has recorded eight wins as a pitcher - demonstrates a similar skill-set to the legendary two-way player Babe Ruth.

Ohtani has been named Most Valuable Player in his league four times, including last season, when the Dodgers became the first franchise in 25 years to win consecutive World Series titles.

Dominican left-fielder Soto became the highest-paid player in baseball history in 2024 when he left the New York Yankees and signed a $765m deal with their bitter cross-city rivals the Mets.

He hit his 250th career home run against the Yankees earlier this season, one of 21 home runs he has delivered in 2026.

Despite Soto's contribution, the Mets narrowly missed out on a post-season berth last year and now sit bottom of the National League East with 43 wins to 60 defeats.

This season, the MLB Bases Covered Live team will again be led by play-by-play announcer Melanie Newman, with former St Louis Cardinals first baseman Xavier Scruggs and Maccabees guitarist Felix White alongside to call the action for seasoned baseball fans and new viewers.

During the 2026 Fifa World Cup, baseball played an unexpectedly large role in the experiences of football fans and players from the UK as they enjoyed memorable outings to ballparks across the US.

After defeating Haiti in their opening game in nearby Foxborough, Scotland's Tartan Army took over Fenway Park in Boston to celebrate while watching the Red Sox take on the Texas Rangers.

England manager Thomas Tuchel threw out the first pitch at Kaufmann Stadium when several members of the England squad watched the Kansas City Royals play the St Louis Cardinals.

fullText:
West Ham have confirmed the sale of winger Crysencio Summerville to Saudi club Al-Hilal.

title: 'Room for improvement' but McClenaghan 2.0 on track
description: Rhys McClenaghan reflects on his qualifying session for the Commonwealth Games pommel horse final on Monday.
fullText:
If Friday's qualifying session was only the start of Rhys McClenaghan "2.0" with his new pommel horse routine that he said would be "a work in progress" at the Commonwealth Games, everyone is in for a treat with what will follow in this rebuild.

Competing on a big stage for the first time in earnest since he peaked when completing the gymnastics 'Grand Slam' by winning Olympic gold in Paris two years ago, McClenaghan showed the big crowd in the Glasgow International Arena what they had been missing during his injury-enforced absence that spanned the entirety of 2025.

The 27-year-old delivered a big score of 14.500 for his routine and celebrated his almost perfect execution (demonstrated by his 9.000 score) with a little dance after stepping off the pommel horse.

McClenaghan exuded confidence on his approach to the apparatus, during his routine and after, when he soaked up the adulation of the crowd that was populated by a strong Northern Ireland contingent.

That is to be expected from an athlete that has won it all in his sport, but despite his perceived assured exterior, McClenaghan was feeling anxious at making his return with all eyes on him and with considerable more pressure than in Birmingham four years ago given his various accolades he has collected since.

"I'd be lying if I said I wasn't nervous, but I'm nervous for every competition, this one held a little bit more weight," he told BBC Sport NI.

"We're at an arena on qualification day and it's packed out, audience cheering when your name is announced and it's a different feeling than other gymnastics competitions.

"Normally qualifications are empty, so it's really nice to be a part of that and it felt like a finals day here and that's why there are a few more smiles and happy faces with how the pommel routine went."

McClenaghan qualifiers for pommel horse final

McClenaghan's score far surpassed the 13.466 and 13.900 that he registered in the two World Cup competitions in Azerbaijan and Antalya as he made his comeback earlier this year.

It is still well short of his personal best achieved at the Olympics final of 15.533, but his polished routine in Glasgow is a step in the right direction and sees him comfortably into Monday's final in third behind Scotland's Reuben Ward and Canada's Jordan Carroll, who both registered 14.550, having had harder difficulty but faring worse on execution than McClenaghan.

Always striving for perfection, the Newtownards man still feels there are elements of his routine that need tweaked, even if they will be minimal adjustments rather than major alterations.

With his great rival Max Whitlock not competing in Glasgow due to injury, McClenaghan now has a real chance to do what he set out to in these games, sandwich the 2022 silver with another gold after triumphing at his first Games in 2018.

"There's more room for improvement," he added.

"I was down on my difficulty score and heat of the moment decisions, I was a bit off balance and too much tension in my arms, so I get the opportunity now to train for Monday's final where I should be a bit more sharp and agile and put out a better routine than I did today."

The only disappointment for McClenaghan on what proved to be a fruitful afternoon, was his failure to reach the floor final.

Competing for the first time since the 2018 Commonwealth Games in the Gold Coast, a stumble as he aimed to land a final triple somersault cost him as he scored 12.350.

It was a rare blemish but he will get back on the (pommel) horse quite literally in Monday's final, which will no doubt help him shelve that disappointment with his eyes on another big prize and the chance to further enhance his legacy.

"I was just happy to be here and compete on floor but at the same time I was here to win medals too, it was a real shame, I was going too much for that stuck landing on the dismount and that had me under rotating.

"The rest of the routine was great and it was nice to get the opportunity to perform it out here."

title: Kim feels 'pretty cool' after carding historic 59
description: Michael Kim is thrilled to be "part of the history books" after a superb 12-under par round of 59 at the 3M Open in Minnesota.
fullText:
Michael Kim is thrilled to be "part of the history books" after a superb 12-under-par round of 59 at the 3M Open in Minnesota.

The American drained a 24-foot birdie putt at the final hole to post just the 16th sub-60 round ever on the US PGA Tour.

Kim birdied the last four holes at TPC Twin Cities course in Blaine, lifting both arms in triumph when the putt on 18 rolled in before unleashing a mighty fist-pump.

The 33-year-old had 12 birdies without a bogey to finish his second round in the lead, three shots in front of compatriot Ben Kohles.

Seoul-born Kim is the 15th golfer to reach the magic number of 59 on the US tour.

Jim Furyk shot a tour-record 58 at the 2016 Travelers Championship, having previously made 59 at the 2013 BMW Championship.

"I kind of remember thinking on 18 that you have to go for it, 60 or 61 doesn't really make too much of a difference," said Kim, whose previous best round was a 62.

"To shoot 59 was pretty cool and feels like I'm part of the history books."

Kim's sensational day included five birdies in a row from the third through the seventh holes, a run launched with an 11-foot birdie putt at the third.

He made a 12-footer at the par-three fourth, landed his approach within five feet and made that at the fifth, sank a 10-foot birdie at the sixth and a two-footer at seven.

Kim added back-to-back birdies at the ninth and 10th and one more at 12 before launching his closing burst with a birdie from just inside 12 feet at the 15th.

He kept it going with a 13-foot birdie at 16 and drilled a 17-foot birdie putt at the par-three 17th.

"I made a really nice birdie putt on 16. It had a lot of break to it and it went in dead centre," Kim said.

"There's a lot of water on 17 and 18 and I just kind of told myself like 'hey, this is the way - this is the moment to get into the history books and let's go for it, let's not try to luck our way into it, let's try to step up and hit some really good shots'."

title: 'I love a good scrap' - Ramsay-Peaty ready for his apprentice
description: Adam Ramsay-Peaty says he expects a "good scrap" as master meets apprentice in the Glasgow swimming pool at the Commonwealth Games on Saturday.
fullText:
Sport is littered with moments when the baton is passed from one generation for the other.

Steffi Graf toppled Martina Navratilova to win her first Grand Slam title on the clay of Paris in 1987 and Jason Kenny beat Chris Hoy to take the coveted sprint spot for Team GB at London 2012.

It is less than a week since Lamine Yamal's Spain beat Lionel Messi's Argentina in another similar moment.

For the youngster involved, it is straightforward: take a shot at the superstar.

The renowned champion has to hold off a rival and time itself.

Scott overcomes pressure and big pal Dean to give Scotland golden start

Horror injury overshadows gymnastics silver at Commonwealths

Adam Ramsay-Peaty becomes the latest to face the latter situation on Saturday - in the 100m breaststroke final at Glasgow's Commonwealth Games, shortly after 21:00 BST.

The greatest breaststroker the world has seen is on his own journey - one which he hopes ends with a third individual gold at the Los Angeles Olympics in two years' time.

Manoeuvring into his slipstream is 18-year-old Filip Nowacki.

Not only has Nowacki started to pick off Ramsay-Peaty's age-group records, he is part of the 31-year-old's AP Race stable - the programme set up to develop the next generation.

Ramsay-Peaty has spoken of wanting to mentor and pass on advice to his young pretender. Last year, Nowacki repaid him by breaking his 100m breaststroke junior British record.

Ramsay-Peaty, who is chasing a 33rd major gold of a glittering career, appeared in no mood to hand over the baton in Friday's semi-finals.

There is uncertainty around a broken finger suffered in June but, side by side in lanes four and five, Ramsay-Peaty built an early lead and held off the youngster in the second length. Nowacki was close but never quite close enough.

"I saw his front wave, but at the same time that is what I train for," Ramsay-Peaty said.

"I know I am a sprinter. I know I can go out fast."

Nowacki, who competes for Jersey here having learned to swim under the tutelage of Nathan Jegou on the Channel Island, is arguably best in the 200m event - a distance Ramsay-Peaty does not race.

In this shorter contest, it is the youngster who should stay stronger for longer.

And when they spoke afterwards alongside each other, Ramsay-Peaty, all chest and tattooed muscle, towered over his young rival - so much so you would be forgiven for thinking the pair compete in different sports.

Nowacki appeared wary of Ramsay-Peaty but there is a cheeky confidence within.

"Course I do," he laughed when asked if he believes he can win.

"No, I wish, I'm gonna give it my best shot" was his quick addition.

Nowacki was not long out of armbands when Ramsay-Peaty won gold in this same pool at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

That was his emergence on to the global stage and two years later the Englishman won his first Olympic title in Rio de Janeiro. Nowacki was only eight years old.

"Adam is a true role model in the sport," Nowacki said.

"I grew up watching him race at Rio, Tokyo and Paris.

"To race him and not be a random competitor but give him a race is special to me."

The pair should compete as Team GB team-mates in LA but are also racing for their own personal ambitions on Saturday.

Despite winning an emotional silver at the Olympics in Paris two years ago, Ramsay-Peaty has not stood atop a major podium since the Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022.

In that meet he won the 50m crown but lost his 100m title to James Wilby. A "self-destructive spiral" amid issues with his mental health, which led to him considering his future in the sport, soon followed.

If Nowacki wins a medal it would be Jersey's first at the Commonwealth Games for 36 years. They have only ever won one gold medal.

Australia's Sam Williamson, who won the first semi-final, will also have something to say.

"It is going to be a good scrap, especially down that last 25m, and I do love a good scrap," Ramsay-Peaty said.

Nowacki hopes to end Jersey's 36-year medal wait

title: Scotland win three medals in 45 minutes to kick-start Glasgow 2026
description: Scotland claim three medals in a magnificent 45 minutes in the pool to kick-start the hosts' Commonwealth Games in fine style in Glasgow.
fullText:
Scotland claimed three medals in a magnificent 45 minutes in the pool to kick-start the hosts' Commonwealth Games in fine style in Glasgow - and added a second gold of the day an hour later to almost take the lid off Tollcross in the city's east end.

Poster boy Duncan Scott started the rush, defending his 200m individual medley gold from Birmingham four years ago by slicing a chunk off his own Games record.

Then Para-swimmer Stephen Clegg added silver in 100m freestyle S13 - with brother James fourth - after battling back from an injury-ravaged year.

And Katie Shanahan upgraded her 2022 Games bronze to silver in the 200m backstroke.

The frenzied scenes around this clammy building eventually abated, only for Faye Rogers to spark more bedlam with a rampant gold in the 200m individual medley SM10.

Scott overcomes pressure and big pal Dean to give Scotland golden start

Horror injury overshadows gymnastics silver at Commonwealths

The drama all unfolded at the same Tollcross pool where 29-year-old Scott won the first of his now 14 Games medals in 2014.

Scotland's most decorated Commonwealth Games athlete was a wee boy then - just 17 - but is a big man now and was under pressure to deliver a first rendition of Flower of Scotland at this staging.

And he delivered sensationally, streaking away from the field in the backstroke and breaststroke legs before closing it out in the freestyle.

Watching from the call room, Clegg could not fail to be roused.

There were times over the past year where the 30-year-old thought he might not be at these Games, and that his swimming career was over.

But he made it to Glasgow and managed to add another silver to the won he claimed in the 50m event four years ago.

Shanahan came home from that Birmingham Games with two surprise bronze medals so silver was an upgrade for another athlete who has come through tough times in recent months.

Her Scottish team-mate Holly McGill just missed out on the medals in fourth.

That success would have been sufficent to sate the home crowd, but Para-athlete Rogers delivered one of the most dominant performances of the night to clinch a second gold for the hosts and spark a second airing of the anthem.

title: Phoenix beat Rockets in high-scoring thriller
description: Joe Clarke and Will Smeed hit fifties as Birmingham Phoenix post the second-highest total in Hundred history to beat Trent Rockets.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Edgbaston

Birmingham Phoenix 214-4 (100 balls): Clarke 68 (33); Harrison 2-27

Trent Rockets 204-7 (100 balls): Banton 67 (32); Tariq 2-36

Birmingham Phoenix won by 10 runs

Birmingham Phoenix and Trent Rockets ended this year's Hundred run-drought with a high-scoring contest at Edgbaston, which the home side edged by 10 runs.

Phoenix posted 214-4 - the second-highest total in the tournament's history behind Oval Invincibles' 226-4 last year - and with Rockets' reply of 204-7, it was the first time that 400 runs have been scored in a game overall.

The 29 sixes hit across both innings was also a Hundred record.

Joe Clarke and Will Smeed both scored fifties in Phoenix's flying start as the pair added 104 from just 49 balls for the first wicket.

After Clarke fell for 68 from 33 balls and Smeed's 51 from 28, Rehan Ahmed and Donovan Ferreira ensured the brilliant start was not in vain.

The pair smashed 63 from just 22 balls for the third wicket, as Ahmed clubbed five sixes in his 25-ball 48 while Ferreira added a valuable cameo off 22 not out from just nine deliveries.

In reply, Rockets made a positive start as openers Finn Allen and Ben Duckett added 65 in 29 balls but the chase started to drift when the pair fell for 43 and 49 respectively.

Tom Banton kept Rockets' hopes alive with a 26-ball fifty, but seamer Scott Currie held his nerve at the death to remove him for 67 with an unlikely 29 needed off the last seven balls and Phoenix closed out the victory.

On a difficult night for bowlers, Rockets spinner Calvin Harrison's figures of 2-27 were an outlier.

Phoenix's innings was the sixth time that 200 has been surpassed in the tournament and sparked some much-needed life into this year's edition after a run of relatively low scores – the previous highest total just 144.

The match also alleviated concerns about the quality of the pitch after Phoenix's women were contrastingly bowled out for 64 earlier in the day.

title: Scott overcomes pressure and big pal Dean to give Scotland golden start
description: Scotland's Duncan Scott thrilled a home crowd with his swim to gold at Tollcross on the first full day of competition at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
Duncan Scott and Tom Dean have won together. They've lost together. They train together in Stirling.

And at a thumping Tollcross on Friday, they stood together on the blocks waiting for the first big swimming final of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow to start.

Scott in lane two. Dean in lane three. Back to back. Little more than a metre between them. But by the end of the 200m individual medley that distance had grown. And grown significantly.

Scotland's poster boy Scott might have only finished little under a second in front of his big pal from England - who had to settle for bronze - but that is a lifetime in the world of elite swimming.

The 29-year-old's time of 1:56.38 was rapid for four lengths of furious thrashing, each one a different stroke.

It was near-enough half a second quicker than the Games record he set in denying Dean gold in Birmingham four years ago.

"I'm pretty happy with that," the never-knowingly overstated Scott told BBC Sport after an emotional rendition of Flower of Scotland. "It was well executed and, to be honest, it's more of a relief rather than anything."

Scotland win three medals in 45 minutes to kick-start Glasgow 2026

Commonwealth Games day one - as it happened

Why is it so special to be part of Team Scotland?

Scott didn't look to be carrying the baggage of expectation when he sauntered out of the call room a little after 19:00 BST, grinning and taking in the splendour of the scenes around him.

But the anticipation of success was there. There among the clammy crowd. There among Team Scotland. And even there among his rivals. After all, he is his country's most decorated Games athlete.

"Duncan had an incredible front end to that race," an upbeat Dean - who moved up to Stirling last year and has struggled badly with injury - told BBC Sport afterwards. "I train with him every day. I know what he does."

Knowing it and doing something about it are different things, though.

Evan Jones gave it a go early on from lane one - touching the wall a fraction in front of his Scotland team-mate after the fly - but then Scott uncorked the good stuff.

His backstroke put him ahead. His breaststroke moved him clear. And he turned for home knowing a fourth Games gold was his.

Dean - who recovered from seventh at halfway - and New Zealand's Lewis Clareburt probably knew it too, but they grafted gamely to keep Scott honest all the way to the wall.

Scott was not being caught, though. Not tonight. Not here. Not with his Scotland kit on and his team looking to him to spark their Games.

A Games which he has backed vocally since Glasgow salvaged it from the wreckage of Victoria's aborted bid.

Almost exactly 12 years after he won his first Commonwealth medal in this very building, he was taking his 14th in his fourth Games. And it was going to be gold.

"I don't usually feel the expectation, but that one I probably did," he told BBC Sport Scotland. "Simply because it's day one and I love representing Scotland and you want to try and get the whole team off to a good start.

"I think there was a bigger picture of trying to get good momentum for the crowd involvement for the rest of the week, and the team as well. So I felt that expectation, but it's nothing I couldn't deal with."

You got the sense there was little that could have discomfited the Alloa native - a momentary loss of his accreditation apart - and even a post-race visit to the drugs testers wasn't going to trouble him.

Scott's got the weekend off now - he's an old boy among the swimming set, after all - but he's more than done his bit to set Glasgow 2026 off on the right note.

title: Hamilton fastest as new Aston Martin makes encouraging debut
description: Lewis Hamilton leads team-mate Charles Leclerc to a Ferrari one-two in Friday practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Ferrari led the field by a significant margin in Friday practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix but Charles Leclerc predicted a "tight" qualifying session on Saturday.

Leclerc trailed team-mate Lewis Hamilton by 0.148 seconds with McLaren's Lando Norris 0.499secs back in third place.

Mercedes had a difficult day, championship leader Kimi Antonelli 13th fastest after a disrupted run on soft tyres and George Russell fifth.

The topic of the day was the new Aston Martin, which Fernando Alonso said felt "much better" after an encouraging debut for the team that has been at the back all season.

The veteran two-time champion was 2.990secs off the pace in 19th place but had a lap faster by 0.4secs ruled out for track limits.

Even so, Alonso's actual lap time marked a major step forward for a team that has been trailing by more than four seconds in recent races.

How to follow Hungarian Grand Prix on the BBC

With a new Honda engine due for the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after Formula 1's summer break, Alonso said there was a "positive atmosphere in the team now".

"The car feels more glued to the ground and easier to drive to an extent when you are in control of the grip in the corners," Alonso added.

"More predictable and an easier car but still a long way to go for us.

"Obviously this will be the first step. We need to find more performance both on the chassis but also on the engine.

"Zandvoort would be a good test for us with the new engine. So step by step but definitely in the right direction."

The key was not only that the upgrade was a step in the right direction but also that it had delivered as expected.

There had been some nervousness around that for the first major upgrade under Adrian Newey's technical leadership. In the past three seasons, upgrades had not delivered as expected, and it was critical for the future that this one, designed and developed with new tools at the team's new factory, worked.

Newey said further upgrades to the car were due for the Italian and Azerbaijan Grands Prix in September.

Alonso said: "We had what we expected in terms of numbers and correlation, which is obviously very encouraging for the future as well, for next year's car and the future upgrades into this year.

"It's still a long way to go for us. Obviously, we're starting so far behind, but this is the first step, hopefully, of good ones coming."

The day was not all positive for Aston Martin, however. Alonso's team-mate Lance Stroll spun out of the first session with what initially appeared to be a rear suspension failure.

He was then unable to take part in the second because there was not enough time to repair the car.

Team representative Pedro de la Rosa said: "It is a suspension failure. We were confident it would not happen in Fernando's car. That's why we sent him out. Because of the lack of spares we couldn't repair his car on time. Some parts need to be repaired and some needed to come here."

Ferrari had been expected to be strong at this track, which is one of the least power-dependent on the calendar, as it has the best car in the corners but it is lacking engine performance.

But Leclerc was cautious about reading too much into it. Hamilton did not speak to the media - only one driver from each team does a pooled interview on Fridays.

"It was a relatively strong day," Leclerc said. "I felt good with the car and the performance seemed to be there straight away so that's a good thing but the weekend is long.

"From the Friday to Saturday we see teams making a jump in performance. Normally we are on the back foot on Friday so it's a good thing we have a good Friday but we still need to stay on it and work hard to get better tomorrow.

"It is going to be tight tomorrow. I don't expect us to have the gap we have today, we will have to do everything perfect. But if the feeling is there I am sure we will do a good job in Q3."

George Russell was 0.933secs off the pace and behind Norris, with a significant upgrade on the McLaren, and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

The Briton said: "It's a bit of a shame because Budapest is one of the most enjoyable circuits to drive. They have resurfaced a third of the track and they've done a really bad job. It's really bumpy.

"The track is braking up in the last corner so people are driving around the middle of the last corner and not hitting the apex.

"The underlying car pace doesn't seem as competitive as we saw in Silverstone and Spa. There is a lot of room to improve. The wind is shifting a lot and that has a real impact into car balance. Hopefully tomorrow will be better."

Antonelli, leading Hamilton by 45 points and Russell by 50, did not complete a qualifying simulation lap in the second session.

His first had to be abandoned when Franco Colapinto crashed his Alpine at the last corner, and his second came to grief when he made an error going into the chicane.

Antonelli was complaining all session about rear brake locking, but he was on a par with Norris' time in the first sector on both laps before they were curtailed.

Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "Lack of grip and balance, both drivers had to wind some front wing out, but on the long runs looked pretty consistent and competitive compared to the Ferrari, Red Bull and McLarens."

Behind Russell, Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was sixth fastest, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and McLaren's Oscar Piastri.

Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.

title: Horror injury overshadows gymnastics silver at Commonwealths
description: A horror fall from England gymnast Gabriel Langton overshadows his team's silver medal in the team event on the opening night of action at Glasgow 2026.
fullText:
A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.

Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.

He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.

Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.

In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance.

"He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."

When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.

Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock, was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.

Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."

Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."

Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one.

"For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."

Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened.

"We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."
